=== P2 statement
# P2: Variance reduction and disposal of initial moduli

Let f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and c=ζ(2)^(−1), where ζ is the Riemann zeta function. For real x≥2 and integers 1≤m≤x define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m). For real 1≤z≤y with Z=f(z)≤Y=f(y)≤x, define V_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}E(x;f(k),l)², T_f(z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)², and S_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{1≤h≤x/f(k)}C_x(hf(k)); all sums over k and h are over positive integers. For every ε>0 there is C(f,ε)>0 such that, uniformly throughout these ranges, |V_f(x;z,y)−[cx(Y−Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)−x²T_f(z,y)]|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/2+ε)+xY^(1−1/d)]. In addition, uniformly for x≥2 and real z≥1 with f(z)≤x, 0≤V_f(x,z)≤C(f,ε)x^(1+ε)f(z)^(2−1/d).
=== P2 proof
# Proof of P2

All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
parameter, as indicated.

**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put

\[
\alpha=1-\frac1d.
\]

There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
that, for every real \(t\ge1\),

\[
 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure

\[
 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
\]

These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).

For the interval in the proposition, write

\[
 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
\]

Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
one each. Consequently,

\[
 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant

\[
 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
\]

satisfies

\[
 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
\]

Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).

We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
a finite \(D_\eta\) such that

\[
 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
\]

Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).

**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
define

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
\]

where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
\]

This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
has absolute value at most

\[
 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
 \le2\sqrt x.
\]

Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),

\[
 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
\]

Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put

\[
 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
\]

By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
in P1 therefore gives the exact identity

\[
 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
                                                                    \tag{7}
\]

Set

\[
 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
\]

The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
\]

There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,

\[
 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
\]

Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if

\[
 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
\]

then (8) proves the uniform estimate

\[
 |M(x;q)|
 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
\]

Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
\]

**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
residue class gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
\]

Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
including for nonintegral \(x\).

Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
\(M(x;q)\), gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
\]

Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly

\[
 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
\]

We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives

\[
 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
 \le3\sqrt x W
 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
\]

The endpoint error in (13) satisfies

\[
 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
\]

For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
\(f(k)\le x\) give

\[
 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
\]

There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields

\[
 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
\]

For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),

\[
 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
\]

The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives

\[
 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
\]

Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
most

\[
 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
\]

Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves

\[
 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
\]

This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).

**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
notation typeset in LaTeX, is:

> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
> number \(\varepsilon\),
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
> \begin{cases}
> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
> \end{cases}
> \]

The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are

> \[
> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
> \]
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
> \]

Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).

We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),

\[
 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
\]

Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that

\[
 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
\]

Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is

\[
 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
\]

The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are

\[
 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
 2-\frac22=1.
\]

It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
such that

\[
 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
\]

The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
image of the relevant supplied PDF page.

**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
weight bound

\[
 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
\]

Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
we obtain

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
\]

To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
\]

Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.

**Source and verification notes.** R. C. Vaughan, *A variance for k-free
numbers in arithmetic progressions* (2005), *Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society* (3) **91**, 573--597,
[DOI:10.1112/S0024611505015352](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352),
was consulted as a bibliographical pointer to the 1998 lemma. The estimate
used in the proof is the verbatim lemma quoted above from the supplied
1998 paper. A bibliographical web search returned post-2010 sources;
reading stopped when their dates were identified, and their content was
excluded from the argument.

A Python sanity check tested (9) and the exact identity (12) for all
integers \(1\le q\le\lfloor x\rfloor\), with
\(x\in\{2,3.25,10,31.75,100,200.5\}\), comprising 346 pairs \((x,q)\).
It used direct squarefree counts and the density formula of P1. Identity
(12) agreed within floating-point tolerance, and every test satisfied
(9). These computations serve only as checks; the proofs of (9) and
(12) are the finite identities and inequalities above.

1	=== P3 statement
2	# P3: Uniform correlation estimate for squarefree numbers
3	
4	For real x≥2 and every integer 1≤m≤x, define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m) and 𝔖(m)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|m}(p²−1)/(p²−2), with products over primes. For every ε>0 there is C(ε)>0 such that |C_x(m)−(x−m)𝔖(m)|≤C(ε)x^(4/5+ε), uniformly for all such x and m. A permitted circle-method cutoff is Q=x^(2/5), for x sufficiently large that Q≤x^(1/2)/2; the major arcs are the subsets of R/Z with |α−a/q|≤Q/(qx), 1≤q≤Q and gcd(a,q)=1. The bound is uniform even when x−m is bounded.
5	=== P3 proof
6	# Proof of P3
7	
8	We prove the stronger bound
9	\[
10	\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
11	\tag{1}
12	\]
13	with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
14	The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
15	No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
16	dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.
17	
18	## An explicit divisor bound
19	
20	Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
21	\(n\). Define the absolute constant
22	\[
23	D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
24	\]
25	where the product is over primes. We will use
26	\[
27	\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
28	\tag{2}
29	\]
30	Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
31	\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
32	then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
33	\[
34	(a+1)p^{-a/10}
35	\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
36	=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
37	\]
38	Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
39	(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
40	all at least one.
41	
42	We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
43	integers \(H\):
44	\[
45	\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
46	\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
47	\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
48	\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
49	\tag{3}
50	\]
51	The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
52	integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
53	Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).
54	
55	## Truncating the square-divisor identities
56	
57	Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
58	\[
59	L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
60	\]
61	In particular,
62	\[
63	\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
64	\tag{4}
65	\]
66	For positive integers \(k\), define
67	\[
68	T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
69	R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
70	\]
71	All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
72	\[
73	\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
74	\tag{5}
75	\]
76	follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
77	least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
78	Also
79	\[
80	|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
81	|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
82	\tag{6}
83	\]
84	
85	For either of the two sets
86	\[
87	I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
88	I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
89	\]
90	there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
91	For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
92	\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
93	\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
94	for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
95	\[
96	\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
97	\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
98	\le\frac{x}{H}.
99	\tag{7}
100	\]
101	This estimate also holds when either set is empty.
102	
103	The exact product identity
104	\[
105	\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
106	=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
107	\]
108	and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
109	most
110	\[
111	|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
112	\]
113	where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
114	\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
115	each of its two terms, yields
116	\[
117	\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
118	\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
119	\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
120	\tag{8}
121	\]
122	In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).
123	
124	## Counting the truncated congruences
125	
126	For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
127	\[
128	n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
129	\]
130	are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
131	both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
132	the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
133	\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
134	\[
135	a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
136	\]
137	Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
138	\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
139	\[
140	h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
141	\]
142	For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
143	number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
144	\[
145	\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
146	-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
147	=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
148	\tag{9}
149	\]
150	This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).
151	
152	Define
153	\[
154	A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
155	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
156	\]
157	Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
158	\[
159	\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
160	\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
161	\tag{10}
162	\]
163	Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
164	at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
165	most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.
166	
167	## The infinite main term and its uniform tail
168	
169	Consider
170	\[
171	A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
172	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
173	\]
174	This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
175	with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
176	absolute sum by
177	\[
178	\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
179	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
180	   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
181	   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
182	\le8.
183	\tag{11}
184	\]
185	
186	We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
187	\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
188	\[
189	\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
190	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
191	  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
192	  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
193	\tag{12}
194	\]
195	For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
196	\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
197	and their total is at most
198	\[
199	\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
200	\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
201	\]
202	For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
203	\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
204	\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
205	\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
206	bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
207	\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
208	bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
209	\[
210	|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
211	=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
212	\tag{13}
213	\]
214	All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
215	\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).
216	
217	Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
218	one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
219	finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
220	exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
221	For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
222	follows:
223	
224	| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
225	| --- | --- | --- |
226	| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
227	| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
228	| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
229	| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |
230	
231	It follows that
232	\[
233	\begin{aligned}
234	A(m)
235	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
236	                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
237	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
238	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
239	  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
240	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
241	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
242	=\mathfrak S(m).
243	\end{aligned}
244	\tag{14}
245	\]
246	The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
247	because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.
248	
249	## Combining the bounds
250	
251	Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
252	\[
253	\begin{aligned}
254	L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
255	&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
256	&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
257	&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
258	\end{aligned}
259	\tag{15}
260	\]
261	For \(x\ge1\),
262	\[
263	\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
264	\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
265	=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
266	\]
267	Thus (15) is at most
268	\[
269	32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
270	\tag{16}
271	\]
272	Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
273	\[
274	\begin{aligned}
275	\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
276	&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
277	&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
278	\end{aligned}
279	\]
280	This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
281	\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
282	\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
283	\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
284	uniformity. \(\square\)

310	# P4: Polynomial averaging with a common density coefficient
311	
312	Let f and ρ be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and put ρ(1)=1. Write ζ for the Riemann zeta function, c=ζ(2)^(−1), and φ for Euler's totient. Define λ(r)=c²φ(r)∏_{p|r}(p²−1)^(−2) when no prime cube divides r, and λ(r)=0 otherwise; the product for r=1 is empty. Define R_f=Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)ρ(r)/r and 𝔖(n)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|n}(p²−1)/(p²−2). 314	# Proof of P4
315	
316	We use P1 exactly as supplied. No external paper is used. All logarithms are natural. Constants introduced below depend only on $f$, except for the absolute constant supplied by P1.
317	
318	## Polynomial bounds and a periodic averaging lemma
319	
320	The leading coefficient of $f$ is positive: otherwise $f(t)\geq 2$ for all $t\geq 1$ would fail. Since $f(t)>0$ on this interval, continuity and the positive limit of $f(t)/t^d$ give constants $a>0$ and $B\geq 1$ such that, for every $t\geq 1$,
321	\[
322	 a t^d\leq f(t)\leq B t^d,
323	 \qquad |f'(t)|\leq B t^{d-1}.
324	 \tag{1}
325	\]
326	When $d\geq 2$, enlarge $B$ so that
327	\[
328	 |f''(t)|\leq B t^{d-2}\quad(t\geq 1).
329	 \tag{2}
330	\]
331	When $d=1$, $f''=0$. Define
332	\[
333	 U=\frac{B}{a},\qquad
334	 V=\frac{B}{a}+\frac{B^2}{a^2},\qquad D=U+V.
335	 \tag{3}
336	\]
337	For $w(t)=f'(t)/f(t)$, equations (1)--(2), including $f''=0$ when $d=1$, imply
338	\[
339	 0<w(t)\leq\frac{U}{t},\qquad
340	 |w'(t)|
341	 \leq\frac{|f''(t)|}{f(t)}+\frac{|f'(t)|^2}{f(t)^2}
342	 \leq\frac{V}{t^2}.
343	 \tag{4}
344	\]
345	Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
346	\[
347	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
348	 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
349	 \leq U(1+\log y)
350	 \leq 2U\log(2x).
351	 \tag{5}
352	\]
353	Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.
354	
355	We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
356	\[
357	 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
358	\]
359	then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
360	\[
361	 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
362	 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
363	 \tag{6}
364	\]
365	To prove this, put
366	\[
367	 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
368	\]
369	Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
370	\[
371	 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
372	 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
373	\]
374	Integration by parts gives the exact identity
375	\[
376	 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
377	 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
378	\]
379	which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.
380	
381	For later use, (4) and (6) yield
382	\[
383	 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
384	       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
385	 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
386	 \tag{7}
387	\]
388	Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
389	\(
390	\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
391	\)
392	These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.
393	
394	## Spectral notation and the common density
395	
396	Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
397	\(
398	\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
399	\)
400	and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
401	\[
402	 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
403	 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
404	 \tag{8}
405	\]
406	In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
407	
408	For $h\geq 1$, define
409	\[
410	 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
411	           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
412	 \tag{9}
413	\]
414	Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
415	\[
416	 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
417	 \tag{10}
418	\]
419	converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
420	\[
421	 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
422	 \tag{11}
423	\]
424	
425	For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
426	\(
427	\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
428	\)
429	into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
430	\[
431	 c_r(n)
432	 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
433	       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
434	 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
435	 \tag{12}
436	\]
437	Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
438	\[
439	 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
440	 \tag{13}
441	\]
442	Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.
443	
444	The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
445	\[
446	 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
447	 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
448	 \tag{14}
449	\]
450	The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
451	\[
452	 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
453	 \qquad
454	 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
455	\]
456	and hence
457	\[
458	 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
459	 \tag{15}
460	\]
461	Put
462	\[
463	 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
464	\]
465	The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
466	\[
467	 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
468	 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
469	 \tag{16}
470	\]
471	
472	Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
473	\[
474	 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
475	 \tag{17}
476	\]
477	No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
478	
479	Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
480	\(
481	c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
482	\)
483	Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
484	\[
485	 \begin{aligned}
486	 (1-p^{-2})^2
487	 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
488	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
489	 &=(1-2p^{-2})
490	       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
491	       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
492	 \end{aligned}
493	 \tag{18}
494	\]
495	This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
496	\(
497	1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
498	\)
499	The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
500	$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
501	\[
502	 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
503	 \qquad
504	 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
505	 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
506	 \tag{19}
507	\]
508	which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.
509	
510	For real $R\geq 2$, set
511	\[
512	 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
513	 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
514	 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
515	\]
516	By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
517	\[
518	 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
519	 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
520	 \tag{20}
521	\]
522	
523	## The first averaging assertion
524	
525	For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
526	\(
527	b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
528	\)
529	has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
530	\[
531	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
532	 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
533	 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
534	 \tag{21}
535	\]
536	The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
537	\[
538	 \begin{aligned}
539	 S_1
540	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
541	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
542	                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
543	 \end{aligned}
544	 \tag{22}
545	\]
546	The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
547	\[
548	 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
549	 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
550	 \tag{23}
551	\]
552	by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.
553	
554	For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
555	\[
556	 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
557	 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
558	 \tag{24}
559	\]
560	For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
561	\[
562	 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
563	 \leq T_R\log(2x),
564	 \tag{25}
565	\]
566	since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
567	\(
568	z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
569	\)
570	Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
571	\[
572	 \boxed{
573	 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
574	 \leq C_0\left(
575	 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
576	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
577	 \right).}
578	 \tag{26}
579	\]

581	## A weight bound for the second assertion
582	
583	Let
584	\[
585	 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
586	\]
587	Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
588	\[
589	 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
590	 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
591	 \tag{27}
592	\]
593	These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
594	\[
595	 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
596	 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
597	 \tag{28}
598	\]
599	Define a constant $K$ by
600	\[
601	 K=
602	 \begin{cases}
603	 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
604	 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
605	 \end{cases}
606	 \tag{29}
607	\]
608	We claim
609	\[
610	 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
611	 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
612	 \tag{30}
613	\]
614	For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
615	\[
616	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
617	\]
618	and
619	\[
620	 \begin{aligned}
621	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
622	 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
623	       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
624	 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
625	       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
626	 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
627	       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
628	 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
629	          xv_h^{d-1}.
630	 \end{aligned}
631	 \tag{31}
632	\]
633	The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
634	\[
635	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
636	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
637	 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
638	 \tag{32}
639	\]

641	
642	Apply (6) to
643	\(
644	b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
645	\)
646	with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
647	\[
648	 \begin{aligned}
649	 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
650	     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
651	   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
652	 &\hspace{15mm}\leq

654	 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
655	 \end{aligned}

657	\]
658	If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.
659	
660	The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
661	\[
662	 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
663	 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
664	 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
665	 \tag{34}
666	\]
667	This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
668	\[
669	 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
670	 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
671	 \tag{35}
672	\]
673	In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.

675	## The second averaging assertion
676	
677	Define the finite approximations
678	\[
679	 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
680	                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
681	 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).

735	 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
736	 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
737	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
738	 \right).}

740	\]
741	
742	Finally, set
743	\[
744	 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.

=== P3 statement
# P3: Uniform correlation estimate for squarefree numbers

For real x≥2 and every integer 1≤m≤x, define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m) and 𝔖(m)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|m}(p²−1)/(p²−2), with products over primes. For every ε>0 there is C(ε)>0 such that |C_x(m)−(x−m)𝔖(m)|≤C(ε)x^(4/5+ε), uniformly for all such x and m. A permitted circle-method cutoff is Q=x^(2/5), for x sufficiently large that Q≤x^(1/2)/2; the major arcs are the subsets of R/Z with |α−a/q|≤Q/(qx), 1≤q≤Q and gcd(a,q)=1. The bound is uniform even when x−m is bounded.
=== P3 proof
# Proof of P3

We prove the stronger bound
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
\tag{1}
\]
with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.

## An explicit divisor bound

Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
\(n\). Define the absolute constant
\[
D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
\]
where the product is over primes. We will use
\[
\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
\tag{2}
\]
Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
\[
(a+1)p^{-a/10}
\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
\]
Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
all at least one.

We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
integers \(H\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
\tag{3}
\]
The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).

## Truncating the square-divisor identities

Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
\[
L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
\]
In particular,
\[
\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
\tag{4}
\]
For positive integers \(k\), define
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
\]
All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
\[
\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
\tag{5}
\]
follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
Also
\[
|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
\tag{6}
\]

For either of the two sets
\[
I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
\]
there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
\[
\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
\le\frac{x}{H}.
\tag{7}
\]
This estimate also holds when either set is empty.

The exact product identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
most
\[
|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
\]
where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
each of its two terms, yields
\[
\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).

## Counting the truncated congruences

For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
\[
n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
\[
a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
\]
Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
\[
h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
\]
For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
\tag{9}
\]
This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).

Define
\[
A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
\[
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.

## The infinite main term and its uniform tail

Consider
\[
A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
absolute sum by
\[
\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
\le8.
\tag{11}
\]

We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
\tag{12}
\]
For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
and their total is at most
\[
\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
\]
For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
\[
|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
\tag{13}
\]
All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).

Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
follows:

| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |

It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(m)
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
=\mathfrak S(m).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.

## Combining the bounds

Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
For \(x\ge1\),
\[
\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
\]
Thus (15) is at most
\[
32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\tag{16}
\]
Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
uniformity. \(\square\)

=== P4 statement
# P4: Polynomial averaging with a common density coefficient

Let f and ρ be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and put ρ(1)=1. Write ζ for the Riemann zeta function, c=ζ(2)^(−1), and φ for Euler's totient. Define λ(r)=c²φ(r)∏_{p|r}(p²−1)^(−2) when no prime cube divides r, and λ(r)=0 otherwise; the product for r=1 is empty. Define R_f=Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)ρ(r)/r and 𝔖(n)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|n}(p²−1)/(p²−2). For h≥1 let v_p(h) be the exponent of p in h, j_p(h)=max{2−v_p(h),0}, and W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{j_p(h)})/(p^{j_p(h)}(p²−2))]. These series and products converge absolutely. For real x≥2, 1≤z≤y, Z=f(z)≤Y=f(y)≤x, and 2≤R≤x, put A=Z^(−1/d)R^(1/2)(log(2R))²+R^(−1/2)(log(2R))²log(2x). There is C(f)>0, uniform throughout these ranges, such that |Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)²−R_f log(Y/Z)|≤C(f)A, and |Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{1≤h≤x/f(k)}(x−hf(k))𝔖(hf(k))−∫_Z^Y Σ_{1≤h≤x/t}(x−ht)W_f(h)dt|≤C(f)x²A. All discrete summation variables are positive integers. No condition on the discriminant, content, or factorization of f is imposed.
=== P4 proof
# Proof of P4

We use P1 exactly as supplied. No external paper is used. All logarithms are natural. Constants introduced below depend only on $f$, except for the absolute constant supplied by P1.

## Polynomial bounds and a periodic averaging lemma

The leading coefficient of $f$ is positive: otherwise $f(t)\geq 2$ for all $t\geq 1$ would fail. Since $f(t)>0$ on this interval, continuity and the positive limit of $f(t)/t^d$ give constants $a>0$ and $B\geq 1$ such that, for every $t\geq 1$,
\[
 a t^d\leq f(t)\leq B t^d,
 \qquad |f'(t)|\leq B t^{d-1}.
 \tag{1}
\]
When $d\geq 2$, enlarge $B$ so that
\[
 |f''(t)|\leq B t^{d-2}\quad(t\geq 1).
 \tag{2}
\]
When $d=1$, $f''=0$. Define
\[
 U=\frac{B}{a},\qquad
 V=\frac{B}{a}+\frac{B^2}{a^2},\qquad D=U+V.
 \tag{3}
\]
For $w(t)=f'(t)/f(t)$, equations (1)--(2), including $f''=0$ when $d=1$, imply
\[
 0<w(t)\leq\frac{U}{t},\qquad
 |w'(t)|
 \leq\frac{|f''(t)|}{f(t)}+\frac{|f'(t)|^2}{f(t)^2}
 \leq\frac{V}{t^2}.
 \tag{4}
\]
Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
 \leq U(1+\log y)
 \leq 2U\log(2x).
 \tag{5}
\]
Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.

We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
\[
 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
\]
then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
\[
 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
 \tag{6}
\]
To prove this, put
\[
 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
\]
Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
\[
 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
\]
Integration by parts gives the exact identity
\[
 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
\]
which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.

For later use, (4) and (6) yield
\[
 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
\(
\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
\)
These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.

## Spectral notation and the common density

Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
\(
\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
\)
and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
\[
 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{8}
\]
In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.

For $h\geq 1$, define
\[
 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
\[
 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
 \tag{10}
\]
converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
\[
 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
 \tag{11}
\]

For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
\(
\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
\)
into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
\[
 c_r(n)
 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
 \tag{12}
\]
Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
\[
 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
 \tag{13}
\]
Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.

The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
\[
 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
\[
 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
 \qquad
 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
\]
and hence
\[
 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
 \tag{15}
\]
Put
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
\[
 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
 \tag{16}
\]

Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
\[
 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
 \tag{17}
\]
No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.

Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
\(
c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
\)
Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (1-p^{-2})^2
 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
 &=(1-2p^{-2})
       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{18}
\]
This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
\(
1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
\)
The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
\[
 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
 \tag{19}
\]
which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.

For real $R\geq 2$, set
\[
 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
\]
By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
\[
 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{20}
\]

## The first averaging assertion

For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
\(
b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
\)
has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
\[
 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
 \tag{21}
\]
The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_1
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{22}
\]
The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
\[
 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
 \tag{23}
\]
by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.

For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
\[
 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
 \tag{24}
\]
For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
\[
 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
 \leq T_R\log(2x),
 \tag{25}
\]
since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
\(
z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
\)
Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
 \leq C_0\left(
 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{26}
\]

## A weight bound for the second assertion

Let
\[
 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
\[
 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{27}
\]
These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
\[
 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
 \tag{28}
\]
Define a constant $K$ by
\[
 K=
 \begin{cases}
 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{29}
\]
We claim
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
 \tag{30}
\]
For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
          xv_h^{d-1}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{31}
\]
The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
\[
 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
 \tag{32}
\]
Thus (30) holds for every $d\geq 1$.

Apply (6) to
\(
b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
\)
with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
 &\hspace{15mm}\leq
 4Kr x v_h^{d-1}
 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{33}
\]
If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.

The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
\[
 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
 \tag{34}
\]
This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
\[
 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
 \tag{35}
\]
In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.

## The second averaging assertion

Define the finite approximations
\[
 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
Equations (8)--(11) give, uniformly for positive integers $n,h$,
\[
 |\mathfrak S(n)-\mathfrak S_R(n)|\leq T_R,
 \qquad |W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\leq T_R.
 \tag{36}
\]

Let $S_2$ denote the discrete expression in the second assertion and $I_2$ its integral expression. Define $S_{2,R}$ and $I_{2,R}$ by replacing $\mathfrak S$ and $W_f$ with $\mathfrak S_R$ and $W_R$, respectively.

For a fixed integer $k$ with $z<k\leq y$, there are
\(
H_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\leq x/f(k)
\)
indices $h$. Before summing over $h$, the error from (36) is at most $T_R f'(k)(x-hf(k))\leq T_R x f'(k)$. After summing over these $H_k$ indices, it is at most
\(
T_R x^2 f'(k)/f(k).
\)
Summing this last bound over at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$ and using (5) gives
\[
 |S_2-S_{2,R}|\leq 2U T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{37}
\]
For each $t\in[Z,Y]$, the $h$-sum has $\lfloor x/t\rfloor\leq x/t$ indices. Before summing, the error in an integrand term is at most $T_R(x-ht)\leq T_R x$. After summing it is at most $T_R x^2/t$. Integration gives
\[
 |I_2-I_{2,R}|
 \leq T_R x^2\int_Z^Y\frac{dt}{t}
 =T_R x^2\log(Y/Z)
 \leq T_R x^2\log(2x).
 \tag{38}
\]

It remains to compare the finite approximations. All relevant sums are finite, so their orders can be interchanged. The change of variables $t=f(u)$ gives, for each $h\leq H$,
\[
 \int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du
 =\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\,dt.
 \tag{39}
\]
Moreover, for integer $k$ in $(z,y]$, the condition $h\leq x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\leq v_h$. Thus (35) compares the entire $h$-sum at a fixed $r$ in $S_{2,R}$ with its counterpart in $I_{2,R}$. Before summing over $r$, its error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ is at most
\(
K_2r\lambda(r)x^2 Z^{-1/d}.
\)
There are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices $r\leq R$; after summing, (20) gives
\[
 |S_{2,R}-I_{2,R}|
 \leq K_2x^2Z^{-1/d}M_R
 \leq C_0K_2 x^2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R.
 \tag{40}
\]
Combining (20) and (37)--(40) proves
\[
 \boxed{
 |S_2-I_2|
 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
 \right).}
 \tag{41}
\]

Finally, set
\[
 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.
\]
With $A$ as in the statement, (26) is the first asserted inequality with right side $C(f)A$, and (41) is the second with right side $C(f)x^2A$. All constants are independent of $x,z,y,R$. Every estimate above is valid on the full stated ranges, including $d=1$ and polynomials with arbitrary content, discriminant, or factorization.

## Numerical sanity checks and source record

A Python check using exact rational arithmetic verified (18) for $p=2,3,5,7,11$ and each of the test densities $0,p^{-2},p^{-1},1$. A separate floating-point check verified the bound (34) for $d=1,\ldots,8$ and $H=1,2,10,1000$. These checks were only sanity checks; (18) and (34) were proved algebraically and by integration above.

The only assumed proposition is the supplied P1. No published source or other run's artifacts were consulted; no excluded source was encountered. There were no supplied objections or previous-proof artifacts for this attempt.

1	=== P5 statement
2	# P5: Dirichlet series, residues, and the explicit constant
3	
4	Let f and ρ be as in problem.md, set ρ(1)=1, and write ζ for the Riemann zeta function. For each prime p define a_p=1+ρ(p²)/(p²(p²−2)), b_p=1+ρ(p)/(p(p²−2)), c_p=1+1/(p²−2), and B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p−a_p)p^(−s)+(c_p−b_p)p^(−2s). Define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))] for positive integers h, where v_p(h) is the exponent of p in h. Put D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), P_f(s)=∏_p(1−2/p²)B_p(s), and H_f(s)=∏_p(1−2/p²)(1−p^(−2s−2))B_p(s). The series for D_f converges absolutely for Re(s)>1; the products for P_f and H_f converge absolutely and locally uniformly for Re(s)>−1/2 and Re(s)>−3/4, respectively. For Re(s)>1, D_f(s)=ζ(s)P_f(s)=ζ(s)ζ(2s+2)H_f(s), and the latter identity continues D_f meromorphically to Re(s)>−3/4. For every fixed σ>−3/4 there is C(f,σ)>0 with |H_f(σ+it)|≤C(f,σ) for all real t. Define R_f=P_f(1), B_f=(γ_E−3/2)R_f+P_f'(1), where γ_E is Euler's constant, and K_f=−(8/3)ζ(−1/2)H_f(−1/2). Then D_f(0)=−1/(2ζ(2)), K_f>0, and R_f=ζ(2)^(−2)∏_p[1+(1−1/p)(ρ(p)+ρ(p²))/(p²−1)²]. This R_f equals Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)ρ(r)/r, where λ(r)=ζ(2)^(−2)φ(r)∏_{p|r}(p²−1)^(−2) for integers r with no prime-cube divisor and is zero otherwise; φ is Euler's totient. Every displayed Euler product specifying R_f or K_f is absolutely convergent.
5	=== P5 proof
6	Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
7	\[

10	For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
11	polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
12	roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
13	\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
14	exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
15	\[
16	0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
17	0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}

20	factorization of \(f\).

22	We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
23	\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
24	\[
25	\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
26	\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
27	=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
28	\]

30	\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
31	\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
32	all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).

179	We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
180	\[
181	A=\prod_p\alpha_p
182	\]
183	exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
184	\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
185	this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
186	\[
187	u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
188	u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).

192	\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}

198	\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers

203	\[
204	\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}

207	\[
208	\begin{aligned}

210	 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}

226	For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
227	absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since

229	\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent

236	For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
237	signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
238	counting function of the positive integers gives
239	\[
240	\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
241	 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
242	       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
243	\]
244	Let
245	\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
246	This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
247	by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
248	integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
249	parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
250	exact identity
251	\[
252	\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
253	 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
254	  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
255	\]
256	The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
257	term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
258	\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
259	Substitution in (19) therefore yields
260	\[
261	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
262	 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
263	       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
264	\]

266	past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
267	at most
268	\[
269	\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
270	\]
271	For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
272	integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)

274	\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the

277	We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),

279	\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
280	\[
281	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}

288	\[
289	\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
290	 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N

414	Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
415	\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between

418	\[
419	v(r)=

500	# P6: Smoothed singular-series sum and the ratio profile
501	
502	Let f and ρ be as in problem.md and put ρ(1)=1. For each integer h≥1 define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))], where products are over primes and v_p(h) is the exponent of p in h. Let D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), initially for Re(s)>1 and then by meromorphic continuation. Define R_f=Res_{s=1}D_f(s), B_f=lim_{s→1}[D_f(s)−R_f/(s−1)]−3R_f/2, K_f=−(16/3)Res_{s=−1/2}D_f(s), and c=ζ(2)^(−1), with ζ the Riemann zeta function. For real H≥1 put Θ_f(H)=Σ_{1≤h≤H}W_f(h)(H−h)²/h and F_f(H)=R_f log H+B_f+c/H−Θ_f(H)/H². There is C(f)>0 such that, uniformly for all real H≥1, |Θ_f(H)−[R_fH²log H+B_fH²+cH−K_fH^(1/2)]|≤C(f)H^(3/8), and consequently |F_f(H)−K_fH^(−3/2)|≤C(f)H^(−13/8). Moreover, uniformly for real x≥2 and 2≤Z≤Y≤x, 2∫_Z^Y Σ_{1≤h≤x/t}(x−ht)W_f(h)dt=Z²Θ_f(x/Z)−Y²Θ_f(x/Y).
503	=== P6 proof
504	# Proof of P6
505	
506	We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
507	`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
508	\[
509	D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
510	\tag{1}
511	\]
512	as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
513	\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
514	are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).
515	
516	## 1. The external statements used
517	
518	The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
519	*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
520	pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
521	as supplied in
522	`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
523	Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
524	typesetting transcribed from the PDF.
525	
526	> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
527	> \[
528	> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
529	> \tag{10.9}
530	> \]
531	
532	> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
533	> \[
534	> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
535	> \]
536	> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
537	> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.
538	
539	Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
540	For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
541	neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
542	strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
543	\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
544	part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
545	\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
546	and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
547	at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.
548	
549	For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
550	\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
551	\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
552	Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
553	\[
554	|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
555	\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
556	\tag{2}
557	\]
558	in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.
559
