=== P5 statement
# P5: Dirichlet series, residues, and the explicit constant

Let f and ρ be as in problem.md, set ρ(1)=1, and write ζ for the Riemann zeta function. For each prime p define a_p=1+ρ(p²)/(p²(p²−2)), b_p=1+ρ(p)/(p(p²−2)), c_p=1+1/(p²−2), and B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p−a_p)p^(−s)+(c_p−b_p)p^(−2s). Define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))] for positive integers h, where v_p(h) is the exponent of p in h. Put D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), P_f(s)=∏_p(1−2/p²)B_p(s), and H_f(s)=∏_p(1−2/p²)(1−p^(−2s−2))B_p(s). The series for D_f converges absolutely for Re(s)>1; the products for P_f and H_f converge absolutely and locally uniformly for Re(s)>−1/2 and Re(s)>−3/4, respectively. For Re(s)>1, D_f(s)=ζ(s)P_f(s)=ζ(s)ζ(2s+2)H_f(s), and the latter identity continues D_f meromorphically to Re(s)>−3/4. For every fixed σ>−3/4 there is C(f,σ)>0 with |H_f(σ+it)|≤C(f,σ) for all real t. Define R_f=P_f(1), B_f=(γ_E−3/2)R_f+P_f'(1), where γ_E is Euler's constant, and K_f=−(8/3)ζ(−1/2)H_f(−1/2). Then D_f(0)=−1/(2ζ(2)), K_f>0, and R_f=ζ(2)^(−2)∏_p[1+(1−1/p)(ρ(p)+ρ(p²))/(p²−1)²]. This R_f equals Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)ρ(r)/r, where λ(r)=ζ(2)^(−2)φ(r)∏_{p|r}(p²−1)^(−2) for integers r with no prime-cube divisor and is zero otherwise; φ is Euler's totient. Every displayed Euler product specifying R_f or K_f is absolutely convergent.
=== P5 proof
Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
\[
C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|,1\}.
\]
For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
\[
0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
\]
These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
factorization of \(f\).

We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
\[
\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
\]
Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
\]
follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
products are holomorphic.

For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
\]
By (1),
\[
\begin{gathered}
0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
\end{gathered}
\]
In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).

The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
\[
w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
\]
respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
\[
1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
\]
The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
\[
\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
\]
It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
\[
\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
\]
More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
\(h>N\) is bounded by
\[
\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
\]
This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).

Write
\[
L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
\]
On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
each individual prime
\[
|L_p(s)-1|
\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
\]
If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
terms, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.

The local factor in \(H_f\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
\[
\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
\]
so its absolute value is at most
\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
\[
2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
\]
and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
summation bounded by
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]
All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
\[
|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
\]
Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
term in its exponent specified in (12).

We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
\[
A=\prod_p\alpha_p
\]
exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
\[
u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
\]
In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
\[
\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
\]
To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
total modulus is at most
\[
\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
\]
This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_f(s)
 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
\(1\), with explicit bound
\[
\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
\]

For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
\[
P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
\]
In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).

For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
counting function of the positive integers gives
\[
\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
\]
Let
\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
exact identity
\[
\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
\]
The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
Substitution in (19) therefore yields
\[
\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
\]
The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
at most
\[
\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
\]
For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).

We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
\[
\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
\]
The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
its coefficient, is bounded by
\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
\(w\to1\) gives
\[
\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
\]
The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
harmonic-sum limit.

Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
\[
\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
\]
The integral has absolute value at most
\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
\[
-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
\]

For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
\[
\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
\]
satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.

At \(s=0\),
\[
L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
\]
The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
so
\[
D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
\]

At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
(16) and (22) show
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
\]
This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
expansion.

At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
\[
M_p(-1/2)
 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
\]
The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
\]
For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
\[
K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
 \prod_p\left\{
 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
\]
The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
\[
\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
\]
The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.

It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_p(1)
 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
                                                               \tag{31}
\end{aligned}
\]
Let
\[
T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
\]
Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
\[
0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
\]
The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
explicitly by
\[
\sum_{p>N}T_p
 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
\]
This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
\(\zeta(2)\) proves
\[
R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
\]

Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
\[
v(r)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
Its first two prime-power values are
\[
v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
\]
For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
by
\[
\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
\]
Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
Euler-product identity
\[
\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
\]
Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
\[
\exp(40C_0/27)
 \left[
 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
 \right].                                         \tag{37}
\]
Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
\[
\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
\]
so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
therefore give the required identity
\[
R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
\]
All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
absolute convergence established above.

No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.

=== P6 statement
# P6: Smoothed singular-series sum and the ratio profile

Let f and ρ be as in problem.md and put ρ(1)=1. For each integer h≥1 define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))], where products are over primes and v_p(h) is the exponent of p in h. Let D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), initially for Re(s)>1 and then by meromorphic continuation. Define R_f=Res_{s=1}D_f(s), B_f=lim_{s→1}[D_f(s)−R_f/(s−1)]−3R_f/2, K_f=−(16/3)Res_{s=−1/2}D_f(s), and c=ζ(2)^(−1), with ζ the Riemann zeta function. For real H≥1 put Θ_f(H)=Σ_{1≤h≤H}W_f(h)(H−h)²/h and F_f(H)=R_f log H+B_f+c/H−Θ_f(H)/H². There is C(f)>0 such that, uniformly for all real H≥1, |Θ_f(H)−[R_fH²log H+B_fH²+cH−K_fH^(1/2)]|≤C(f)H^(3/8), and consequently |F_f(H)−K_fH^(−3/2)|≤C(f)H^(−13/8). Moreover, uniformly for real x≥2 and 2≤Z≤Y≤x, 2∫_Z^Y Σ_{1≤h≤x/t}(x−ht)W_f(h)dt=Z²Θ_f(x/Z)−Y²Θ_f(x/Y).
=== P6 proof
# Proof of P6

We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
\tag{1}
\]
as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).

## 1. The external statements used

The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
as supplied in
`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
typesetting transcribed from the PDF.

> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
> \[
> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
> \tag{10.9}
> \]

> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
> \[
> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
> \]
> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.

Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.

For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
\[
|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
\tag{2}
\]
in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.

## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip

562	We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
563	on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
564	the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
565	\[
566	\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
567	       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
568	       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.

741	\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
742	       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
743	=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
744	\]
745	because each of
746	\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
747	\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
748	A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
749	\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
750	are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
751	the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).
752	
753	Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
754	positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
755	\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
756	On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
757	\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
758	\[
759	\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
760	\]
761	Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
762	it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
763	segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
764	justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
765	\[
766	\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
767	\qquad
768	G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
769	\tag{12}
770	\]
771	The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
772	weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).
773	
774	Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
775	\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
776	\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
777	(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
778	checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
779	pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.
780	
781	Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
782	\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
783	least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
784	Thus (10) gives the bound
785	\[
786	|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
787	                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
788	\]
789	Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
790	over both segments, the bound is at most
791	\[
792	\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
793	\]
794	which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
795	asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.
796	
797	For that vertical line define the finite constant
798	\[
799	M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
800	\]
801	It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
802	(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
803	\[
804	|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
805	\]
806	The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
807	integrand is bounded by
808	\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
809	\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
810	tail, (10) gives
811	\[
812	|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
813	\qquad(|t|\geq2).
814	\]
815	After integration over both tails the bound is
816	\[
817	4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
818	=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.

820	In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
821	\[
822	\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
823	                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
824	\leq C_*H^{3/8},
825	\tag{13}
826	\]
827	where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
828	\[
829	C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
830	       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
831	                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
832	\tag{14}
833	\]
834	The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
835	just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
836	left integral.

838	## 4. Residues and the two estimates
839	
840	Write the Laurent expansion at one as
841	\[
842	D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
843	\]
844	Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
845	gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
846	about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
847	with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
848	by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
849	local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.
850	
851	Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
852	\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
853	\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
854	\[
855	H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
856	=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
857	\tag{15}
858	\]
859	At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
860	\[
861	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
862	=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
863	\tag{16}
864	\]
865	At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
866	Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
867	\[
868	\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
869	=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
870	=-K_fH^{1/2}.
871	\tag{17}
872	\]
873	This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
874	\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
875	\[
876	-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
877	=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
878	\]
879	
880	Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
881	Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
882	\[
883	\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
884	\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
885	\tag{18}
886	\]
887	for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
888	an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
889	The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
890	the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
891	\[
892	F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
893	\]
894	Therefore
895	\[
896	|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
897	\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
898	\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
899	\]
900	which proves the second assertion with the same constant.

902	## 5. The integral identity
903	
904	Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
905	\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
906	term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
907	\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
908	finite sum identity
909	\[
910	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
911	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
912	                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
913	\tag{19}
914	\]
915	For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
916	\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
917	\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
918	integral is exactly
919	\[
920	2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
921	=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
922	\tag{20}
923	\]
924	Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
925	\[
926	Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
927	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
928	\]
929	and
930	\[
931	Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
932	=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
933	\]
934	In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
935	extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
936	zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
937	\[
938	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
939	=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
940	\]
941	This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.

972	=== P7 statement
973	# P7: Assembly and uniform error budget
974	
975	Let f and V_f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, Y=f(y), and η_d=min{1/5,1/(4d−1)}. Define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))], with ρ(1)=1 and v_p(h) the exponent of p in h. Let D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), continued meromorphically; put R_f=Res_{s=1}D_f(s), B_f=lim_{s→1}[D_f(s)−R_f/(s−1)]−3R_f/2, K_f=−(16/3)Res_{s=−1/2}D_f(s), Θ_f(H)=Σ_{1≤h≤H}W_f(h)(H−h)²/h, and F_f(H)=R_f log H+B_f+1/(ζ(2)H)−Θ_f(H)/H². For every 0<ε<η_d/2 there are C(f,ε)>0 and x_0(f,ε) such that, uniformly for real x≥x_0 and y≥1 with Y≤x, |V_f(x,y)−x²F_f(x/Y)|≤C(f,ε)x^(2−η_d+ε) and |V_f(x,y)−K_f x^(1/2)Y^(3/2)|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/8)Y^(13/8)+x^(2−η_d+ε)]. Permitted auxiliary choices for Y≥x^θ are θ=2d/(4d−1), Z=x^θ, the real z≥1 satisfying f(z)=Z, and R=Z^(1/d) in P4; for Y<Z the initial-modulus bound applies directly. All constants may depend only on the indicated f and ε.
976	=== P7 proof
977	# Proof of P7
978	
979	We use the supplied propositions P2–P6 as black boxes. No external literature
980	is used. Write
981	\[
982	c=\zeta(2)^{-1},\qquad
983	a=4d-1,\qquad \theta=\frac{2d}{a},\qquad
984	\eta=\min\left\{\frac15,\frac1a\right\}.
985	\]
986	Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\eta/2\), and set
987	\(\delta=\varepsilon/2\). Every constant below is independent of \(x,y\);
988	constants denoted by \(C_f\) depend only on \(f\), and those denoted by
989	\(C_{f,\varepsilon}\) depend only on \(f,\varepsilon\). Constants may be
990	enlarged from one occurrence to the next.
991	
992	## Polynomial bounds and identification of the density
993	
994	The assumptions in problem.md are \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\), \(d\ge1\),
995	\(f(t)\ge2\), and \(f'(t)\ge1\) for every real \(t\ge1\).
996	The leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive, because \(f(t)\ge2\) on
997	this half-line. The functions \(f(t)/t^d\) and
998	\(f'(t)/t^{d-1}\) tend to positive limits as \(t\to\infty\).
999	Continuity on each bounded closed subinterval of \([1,\infty)\), and
1000	the positivity assumptions, therefore give constants \(b_f,B_f^*>0\)
1001	such that
1002	\[
1003	b_f t^d\le f(t)\le B_f^*t^d,
1004	\qquad 0<f'(t)\le B_f^*t^{d-1}\quad(t\ge1).
1005	\tag{1}
1006	\]
1007	Here \(B_f^*\) is just a bound, distinct from the constant \(B_f\)
1008	in the statement. In particular,
1009	\[
1010	\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le \frac{B_f^*}{b_f k}\quad(k\ge1),
1011	\qquad y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\quad\text{if }f(y)\le x.
1012	\tag{2}
1013	\]
1014	
1015	The coefficient of \(\log(Y/Z)\) in P4 is the \(R_f\) in the
1016	statement. Indeed, P5 gives
1017	\[
1018	D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad
1019	P_f(1)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
1020	\]
1021	Its asserted convergence makes \(P_f\) holomorphic near \(1\), so the
1022	residue at \(1\) is \(P_f(1)\), which is exactly the coefficient in
1023	P4. All the definitions of \(W_f,\Theta_f,F_f,R_f,B_f,K_f\) in P6
1024	are those in P7. Thus P6 applies with these definitions and yields a
1025	constant \(C_f\) such that
1026	\[
1027	\left|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}\right|\le C_fH^{-13/8}
1028	\quad(H\ge1).
1029	\tag{3}
1030	\]
1031	Since \(H^{-13/8}\le H^{-3/2}\) for \(H\ge1\), enlarging the
1032	constant to include \(|K_f|\) gives
1033	\[
1034	|F_f(H)|\le C_fH^{-3/2}\quad(H\ge1).
1035	\tag{4}
1036	\]
1037	
1038	## Reduction on an interval of moduli
1039	
1040	For the moment let \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
1041	\(2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\).
1042	Put
1043	\[
1044	\begin{split}
1045	M(x;z,y)&=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)
1046	  \sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}(x-hf(k))\mathfrak S(hf(k)),\\
1047	I(x;Z,Y)&=\int_Z^Y
1048	  \sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt,\\
1049	A(x,Z,R)&=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
1050	       +R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x).
1051	\end{split}
1052	\tag{5}
1053	\]
1054	All discrete variables in these expressions are positive integers.
1055	
1056	We first record the correlation error with both summation lengths.
1057	For a fixed integer \(k\) with \(z<k\le y\), there are
1058	\(N_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\le x/f(k)\) choices of \(h\).
1059	For each choice, \(m=hf(k)\) is an integer satisfying
1060	\(1\le m\le x\): integrality follows from \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\),
1061	and the upper bound follows from the restriction on \(h\).
1062	Consequently P3 with exponent \(\delta\) bounds each unweighted
1063	correlation error by \(C_\delta x^{4/5+\delta}\). After multiplication
1064	by the positive weight \(f'(k)\) and summation over these \(N_k\)
1065	values, the error is at most
1066	\[
1067	C_\delta f'(k)N_kx^{4/5+\delta}
1068	\le C_\delta x^{9/5+\delta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}.
1069	\tag{6}
1070	\]
1071	There are \(\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor\le\lfloor y\rfloor
1072	\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) possible values of \(k\). Use (2) to sum (6):
1073	\[
1074	\begin{split}
1075	|S_f(x;z,y)-M(x;z,y)|
1076	&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}
1077	       \sum_{1\le k\le y}\frac1k\\
1078	&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}(1+\log y)\\
1079	&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x).
1080	\end{split}
1081	\tag{7}
1082	\]
1083	The last inequality uses \(y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\), with its
1084	constant depending only on \(f\).
1085	
1086	P4, applied with precisely the ranges preceding (5), gives the two
1087	errors
1088	\[
1089	|M(x;z,y)-I(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2A(x,Z,R),
1090	\qquad
1091	|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_fA(x,Z,R).
1092	\tag{8}
1093	\]
1094	The hypotheses needed here are exactly \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
1095	\(Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\), together
1096	with the polynomial assumptions already checked. No extra arithmetic
1097	assumption on \(f\) is being introduced.
1098	
1099	Use P2 with exponent \(\delta\), substitute (7) and (8), and retain
1100	the factors \(2\) and \(x^2\) multiplying the errors of \(S_f\) and
1101	\(T_f\). This gives
1102	\[
1103	\begin{split}
1104	\big|V_f(x;z,y)-[cx(Y-Z)+2I(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)]\big|
1105	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}
1106	  +xY^{1-1/d}\\
1107	 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
1108	\end{split}
1109	\tag{9}
1110	\]
1111	More explicitly, the two substitutions in the \(S_f\) term contribute
1112	at most \(2C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)
1113	+2C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\), and the substitution in the \(T_f\) term
1114	contributes at most \(C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\). These are the last two
1115	terms on the right of (9), after enlarging its constant.
1116	
1117	The integral identity in P6 is applicable because \(2\le Z\le Y\le x\).
1118	It is exact:
1119	\[
1120	2I(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
1121	\tag{10}
1122	\]
1123	From the definition of \(F_f\), direct subtraction gives the exact
1124	identity
1125	\[
1126	\begin{split}
1127	x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)
1128	={}&-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)\\
1129	 &+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
1130	\end{split}
1131	\tag{11}
1132	\]
1133	In particular the \(B_f\) terms cancel. Combining (9)–(11) proves
1134	\[
1135	\begin{split}
1136	\big|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)\big|
1137	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}\\
1138	 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
1139	\end{split}
1140	\tag{12}
1141	\]
1142	
1143	## The cutoff and its error budget
1144	
1145	Take
1146	\[
1147	Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
1148	\tag{13}
1149	\]
1150	We have \(0<\theta<1\) and \(0<2/a<1\) for every integer
1151	\(d\ge1\). Choose \(x_0=x_0(f,\varepsilon)\ge2\) large enough
1152	that \(Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}\) and \(R\ge2\) whenever
1153	\(x\ge x_0\). Then \(Z\le x\) and \(R\le x\).
1154	Since \(f'(t)\ge1\) for \(t\ge1\), the polynomial is strictly
1155	increasing there, continuous, and unbounded. Hence there is a unique
1156	real \(z\ge1\) with \(f(z)=Z\). If \(Y\ge Z\), strict
1157	monotonicity gives \(z\le y\), so every hypothesis used for (12)
1158	holds for the choices (13).
1159	
1160	The powers in \(A\) are
1161	\[
1162	Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=x^{-2/a}x^{1/a}=x^{-1/a},
1163	\qquad R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}.
1164	\]
1165	As \(R\le x\), the two terms of \(A\), separately, satisfy
1166	\[
1167	\begin{split}
1168	Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
1169	 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^2,\\
1170	R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x)
1171	 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
1172	\end{split}
1173	\]
1174	It follows that
1175	\[
1176	x^2A(x,Z,R)\le Cx^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
1177	\tag{14}
1178	\]
1179	
1180	The initial-modulus estimate in P2, with exponent \(\delta\), applies
1181	to this \(z\), since \(z\ge1\) and \(f(z)=Z\le x\). It gives
1182	\[
1183	0\le V_f(x,z)
1184	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}
1185	=C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-1/a+\delta},
1186	\tag{15}
1187	\]
1188	where the exponent calculation is
1189	\[
1190	1+\theta(2-1/d)=1+\frac{4d-2}{a}=2-\frac1a.
1191	\tag{16}
1192	\]
1193	The other boundary contribution is controlled by (4), because \(x/Z\ge1\):
1194	\[
1195	x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}
1196	=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}.
1197	\tag{17}
1198	\]
1199	For all \(d\ge1\),
1200	\[
1201	\left(2-\frac1a\right)-\left(\frac12+\frac{3d}{a}\right)
1202	=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
1203	\tag{18}
1204	\]
1205	Thus (17) is at most \(C_fx^{2-1/a}\).
1206	
1207	Here is the complete comparison of the errors in (12), (15), and
1208	(17) with the target exponent. For \(x\ge2\),
1209	\[
1210	\begin{aligned}
1211	x^{3/2+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
1212	&&\text{since }\eta\le1/5\text{ and }\delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
1213	xY^{1-1/d}&\le x^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-\eta},
1214	&&\text{since }Y\le x,\ 1-1/d\ge0,\ 1/d\ge\eta,\\
1215	x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)&\le
1216	 C_\varepsilon x^{9/5+\varepsilon}
1217	 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
1218	&&\text{since }\log(2x)\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/5,\\
1219	x^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3&\le
1220	 C_\varepsilon x^{2-1/a+\varepsilon/2}
1221	 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
1222	&&\text{since }(\log(2x))^3\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/a,\\
1223	x^{2-1/a+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
1224	&&\text{since }\eta\le1/a,\ \delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
1225	x^{1/2+3d/a}&\le x^{2-1/a}\le x^{2-\eta},
1226	&&\text{by (18) and }\eta\le1/a.
1227	\end{aligned}
1228	\tag{19}
1229	\]
1230	The logarithm bounds used here follow, for any fixed positive power
1231	\(u\), from boundedness of \((\log(2x))^j/x^u\) on \([2,\infty)\)
1232	for \(j=1,3\). Their constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
1233	
1234	For \(Y\ge Z\), the defining sums split exactly as
1235	\[
1236	V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y).
1237	\]
1238	Subtracting \(x^2F_f(x/Y)\), using (12), and then applying
1239	(14)–(19) gives
1240	\[
1241	\begin{split}
1242	|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|
1243	&\le V_f(x,z)+x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\\
1244	&\quad+C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}
1245	       +x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big]\\
1246	&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.
1247	\end{split}
1248	\tag{20}
1249	\]
1250	
1251	## Moduli below the cutoff
1252	
1253	Suppose instead that \(Y<Z=x^\theta\). Apply the initial-modulus
1254	bound in P2 directly with its argument \(z\) equal to \(y\).
1255	Its hypotheses hold because \(y\ge1\) and \(f(y)=Y\le x\).
1256	The exponent \(2-1/d\) is positive, so (16) gives
1257	\[
1258	0\le V_f(x,y)
1259	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Y^{2-1/d}
1260	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}
1261	=C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-1/a+\delta}.
1262	\tag{21}
1263	\]
1264	Also \(x/Y\ge1\), so (4) and (18) imply
1265	\[
1266	x^2|F_f(x/Y)|
1267	\le C_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}
1268	\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}
1269	=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}
1270	\le C_fx^{2-1/a}.
1271	\tag{22}
1272	\]
1273	The triangle inequality, (21), (22), and \(\eta\le1/a\) therefore
1274	give
1275	\[
1276	|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|
1277	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.
1278	\tag{23}
1279	\]
1280	Together, (20) and (23) prove the first assertion uniformly for all
1281	the required \(x,y\).
1282	
1283	## The power main term
1284	
1285	For every \(Y\le x\), apply (3) with \(H=x/Y\ge1\) and multiply
1286	by \(x^2\). Tracking the powers gives
1287	\[
1288	\begin{split}
1289	\left|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\right|
1290	&\le C_fx^2(x/Y)^{-13/8}\\
1291	&=C_fx^{3/8}Y^{13/8},
1292	\end{split}
1293	\tag{24}
1294	\]
1295	where \(x^2(x/Y)^{-3/2}=x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\) identifies the main term.
1296	Combining (24) with the first assertion proves
1297	\[
1298	\left|V_f(x,y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\right|
1299	\le C_{f,\varepsilon}
1300	\left[x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}\right].
1301	\]
1302	Enlarge one constant to cover both asserted inequalities. The choices
1303	of \(x_0\) and all constants made above depend only on \(f\) and
1304	\(\varepsilon\), as required. No numerical sanity checks were used
1305	in this proof.
1306	=== P7 reviews

1308	  "verdict": "pass",
1309	  "severity": "cosmetic",
1310	  "location": "No step fails. The minor points are the unused count \"There are \u230ay\u230b\u2212\u230az\u230b \u2264 \u230ay\u230b \u2264 b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d} possible values of k\" before (7), and the unlabelled constant C in (14).",

P5 gives D_f=\u03b6P_f for Re s>1, and P_f is holomorphic on Re s>\u22121/2. So Res_{s=1}D_f=P_f(1)=\u03a3\u03bb(r)\u03c1(r)/r, which is the coefficient in P4. B_f and K_f are defined identically in P6 and in the statement.\n\n(ii) Hypotheses of P2, P3, P4 and P6 at the choices Z=x^\u03b8, R=x^{2/a}. These hold once x_0(f) makes Z\u22652 and R\u22652: \u03b8<1 and 2/a<1, z\u22651 exists because f is increasing with f(1)\u2264Z, and every m=hf(k) satisfies m\u2264x.\n\n(iii) The summed P3 error is right: f'(k)N_k x^{4/5+\u03b4}\u2264x^{9/5+\u03b4}f'(k)/f(k)\u226ax^{9/5+\u03b4}/k, and summing over k\u2264y\u226ax^{1/d} gives x^{9/5+\u03b4}log(2x).\n\n(iv) Identity (11) is correct: x\u00b2(F(x/Y)\u2212F(x/Z)) = \u2212x\u00b2R_f log(Y/Z)+cx(Y\u2212Z)+Z\u00b2\u0398(x/Z)\u2212Y\u00b2\u0398(x/Y). I also re-derived P6's integral identity: \u222b_Z^{x/h}(x\u2212ht)dt=(x\u2212hZ)\u00b2/(2h).\n\n(v) Exponent bookkeeping:\n- 1+\u03b8(2\u22121/d)=(8d\u22123)/a=2\u22121/a.\n- Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}.\n- (2\u22121/a)\u2212(1/2+3d/a)=(6d\u22125)/(2a)>0.\n- x\u00b2(x/Y)^{-13/8}=x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}.\n- Every term in (19) is \u2264x^{2\u2212\u03b7+\u03b5}, since \u03b7\u22641/5, \u03b7\u22641/a\u22641/d and \u03b4=\u03b5/2.\n\n(vi) The case Y<Z is handled by P2's initial-modulus bound together with (4). ## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip

We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
\[
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.

Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
and after summation its modulus is at most
\[
\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
\]
The other two terms satisfy
\[
\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
\]
and
\[
\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
\]
Consequently, with the explicit constants
\[
C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
\]
we have
\[
|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
\tag{4}
\]

Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
\[
|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
\]
For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\zeta(s)|
&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
\(2T\geq4\). Thus
\[
|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
\tag{5}
\]

We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
\[
0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
\tag{6}
\]
Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{7}
\]
For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
\[
q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
\]
whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.

Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
\[
L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
\]
Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The prime sum of these bounds is at most
\[
(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
=2(6+17d).
\]
Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
bounded by the following finite number:
\[
U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
\]
After multiplication their modulus is at most
\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
Therefore
\[
|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
\qquad
M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
\tag{9}
\]
Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
\[
C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
\]
We then have the explicit growth estimate
\[
|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
\tag{10}
\]
where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).

## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement

The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
\[
\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]
For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
\[
\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
\]
because each of
\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).

Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
\[
\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
\]
Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
\[
\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
\qquad
G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
\tag{12}
\]
The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).

Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.

Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
Thus (10) gives the bound
\[
|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
\]
Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
over both segments, the bound is at most
\[
\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
\]
which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.

For that vertical line define the finite constant
\[
M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
\]
It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
\[
|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
\]
The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
integrand is bounded by
\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
tail, (10) gives
\[
|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
\qquad(|t|\geq2).
\]
After integration over both tails the bound is
\[
4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
\]
In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
\[
\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
\leq C_*H^{3/8},
\tag{13}
\]
where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
\[
C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
left integral.

## 4. Residues and the two estimates

Write the Laurent expansion at one as
\[
D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
\]
Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.

Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
\[
H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
\tag{15}
\]
At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
\tag{16}
\]
At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-K_fH^{1/2}.
\tag{17}
\]
This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
\[
-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
\]

Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
\[
\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
\tag{18}
\]
for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
\[
F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
\]
which proves the second assertion with the same constant.

## 5. The integral identity

Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
finite sum identity
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
\tag{19}
\]
For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
integral is exactly
\[
2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
\tag{20}
\]
Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
\[
Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
\]
and
\[
Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
\]
In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\]
This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.

=== P7 statement
# P7: Assembly and uniform error budget

Let f and V_f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, Y=f(y), and η_d=min{1/5,1/(4d−1)}. Define W_f(h)=∏_p(1−2/p²)[1+ρ(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}})/(p^{max{2−v_p(h),0}}(p²−2))], with ρ(1)=1 and v_p(h) the exponent of p in h. Let D_f(s)=Σ_{h≥1}W_f(h)h^(−s), continued meromorphically; put R_f=Res_{s=1}D_f(s), B_f=lim_{s→1}[D_f(s)−R_f/(s−1)]−3R_f/2, K_f=−(16/3)Res_{s=−1/2}D_f(s), Θ_f(H)=Σ_{1≤h≤H}W_f(h)(H−h)²/h, and F_f(H)=R_f log H+B_f+1/(ζ(2)H)−Θ_f(H)/H². For every 0<ε<η_d/2 there are C(f,ε)>0 and x_0(f,ε) such that, uniformly for real x≥x_0 and y≥1 with Y≤x, |V_f(x,y)−x²F_f(x/Y)|≤C(f,ε)x^(2−η_d+ε) and |V_f(x,y)−K_f x^(1/2)Y^(3/2)|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/8)Y^(13/8)+x^(2−η_d+ε)]. Permitted auxiliary choices for Y≥x^θ are θ=2d/(4d−1), Z=x^θ, the real z≥1 satisfying f(z)=Z, and R=Z^(1/d) in P4; for Y<Z the initial-modulus bound applies directly. All constants may depend only on the indicated f and ε.
=== P7 proof
# Proof of P7

We use the supplied propositions P2–P6 as black boxes. No external literature
is used. Write
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1},\qquad
a=4d-1,\qquad \theta=\frac{2d}{a},\qquad
\eta=\min\left\{\frac15,\frac1a\right\}.
\]
Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\eta/2\), and set
\(\delta=\varepsilon/2\). Every constant below is independent of \(x,y\);
constants denoted by \(C_f\) depend only on \(f\), and those denoted by
\(C_{f,\varepsilon}\) depend only on \(f,\varepsilon\). Constants may be
enlarged from one occurrence to the next.

## Polynomial bounds and identification of the density

The assumptions in problem.md are \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\), \(d\ge1\),
\(f(t)\ge2\), and \(f'(t)\ge1\) for every real \(t\ge1\).
The leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive, because \(f(t)\ge2\) on
this half-line. The functions \(f(t)/t^d\) and
\(f'(t)/t^{d-1}\) tend to positive limits as \(t\to\infty\).
Continuity on each bounded closed subinterval of \([1,\infty)\), and
the positivity assumptions, therefore give constants \(b_f,B_f^*>0\)
such that
\[
b_f t^d\le f(t)\le B_f^*t^d,
\qquad 0<f'(t)\le B_f^*t^{d-1}\quad(t\ge1).
\tag{1}
\]
Here \(B_f^*\) is just a bound, distinct from the constant \(B_f\)
in the statement. In particular,
\[
\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le \frac{B_f^*}{b_f k}\quad(k\ge1),
\qquad y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\quad\text{if }f(y)\le x.
\tag{2}
\]

The coefficient of \(\log(Y/Z)\) in P4 is the \(R_f\) in the
statement. Indeed, P5 gives
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad
P_f(1)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
\]
Its asserted convergence makes \(P_f\) holomorphic near \(1\), so the
residue at \(1\) is \(P_f(1)\), which is exactly the coefficient in
P4. All the definitions of \(W_f,\Theta_f,F_f,R_f,B_f,K_f\) in P6
are those in P7. Thus P6 applies with these definitions and yields a
constant \(C_f\) such that
\[
\left|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}\right|\le C_fH^{-13/8}
\quad(H\ge1).
\tag{3}
\]
Since \(H^{-13/8}\le H^{-3/2}\) for \(H\ge1\), enlarging the
constant to include \(|K_f|\) gives
\[
|F_f(H)|\le C_fH^{-3/2}\quad(H\ge1).
\tag{4}
\]

## Reduction on an interval of moduli

For the moment let \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
\(2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\).
Put
\[
\begin{split}
M(x;z,y)&=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)
  \sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}(x-hf(k))\mathfrak S(hf(k)),\\
I(x;Z,Y)&=\int_Z^Y
  \sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt,\\
A(x,Z,R)&=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
       +R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x).
\end{split}
\tag{5}
\]
All discrete variables in these expressions are positive integers.

We first record the correlation error with both summation lengths.
For a fixed integer \(k\) with \(z<k\le y\), there are
\(N_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\le x/f(k)\) choices of \(h\).
For each choice, \(m=hf(k)\) is an integer satisfying
\(1\le m\le x\): integrality follows from \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\),
and the upper bound follows from the restriction on \(h\).
Consequently P3 with exponent \(\delta\) bounds each unweighted
correlation error by \(C_\delta x^{4/5+\delta}\). After multiplication
by the positive weight \(f'(k)\) and summation over these \(N_k\)
values, the error is at most
\[
C_\delta f'(k)N_kx^{4/5+\delta}
\le C_\delta x^{9/5+\delta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}.
\tag{6}
\]
There are \(\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor\le\lfloor y\rfloor
\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) possible values of \(k\). Use (2) to sum (6):
\[
\begin{split}
|S_f(x;z,y)-M(x;z,y)|
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}
       \sum_{1\le k\le y}\frac1k\\
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}(1+\log y)\\
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x).
\end{split}
\tag{7}
\]
The last inequality uses \(y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\), with its
constant depending only on \(f\).

P4, applied with precisely the ranges preceding (5), gives the two
errors
\[
|M(x;z,y)-I(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2A(x,Z,R),
\qquad
|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_fA(x,Z,R).
\tag{8}
\]
The hypotheses needed here are exactly \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
\(Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\), together
with the polynomial assumptions already checked. No extra arithmetic
assumption on \(f\) is being introduced.

Use P2 with exponent \(\delta\), substitute (7) and (8), and retain
the factors \(2\) and \(x^2\) multiplying the errors of \(S_f\) and
\(T_f\). This gives
\[
\begin{split}
\big|V_f(x;z,y)-[cx(Y-Z)+2I(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)]\big|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}
  +xY^{1-1/d}\\
 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
\end{split}
\tag{9}
\]
More explicitly, the two substitutions in the \(S_f\) term contribute
at most \(2C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)
+2C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\), and the substitution in the \(T_f\) term
contributes at most \(C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\). These are the last two
terms on the right of (9), after enlarging its constant.

The integral identity in P6 is applicable because \(2\le Z\le Y\le x\).
It is exact:
\[
2I(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\tag{10}
\]
From the definition of \(F_f\), direct subtraction gives the exact
identity
\[
\begin{split}
x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)
={}&-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)\\
 &+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\end{split}
\tag{11}
\]
In particular the \(B_f\) terms cancel. Combining (9)–(11) proves
\[
\begin{split}
\big|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)\big|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}\\
 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
\end{split}
\tag{12}
\]

## The cutoff and its error budget

Take
\[
Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
\tag{13}
\]
We have \(0<\theta<1\) and \(0<2/a<1\) for every integer
\(d\ge1\). Choose \(x_0=x_0(f,\varepsilon)\ge2\) large enough
that \(Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}\) and \(R\ge2\) whenever
\(x\ge x_0\). Then \(Z\le x\) and \(R\le x\).
Since \(f'(t)\ge1\) for \(t\ge1\), the polynomial is strictly
increasing there, continuous, and unbounded. Hence there is a unique
real \(z\ge1\) with \(f(z)=Z\). If \(Y\ge Z\), strict
monotonicity gives \(z\le y\), so every hypothesis used for (12)
holds for the choices (13).

The powers in \(A\) are
\[
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=x^{-2/a}x^{1/a}=x^{-1/a},
\qquad R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}.
\]
As \(R\le x\), the two terms of \(A\), separately, satisfy
\[
\begin{split}
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^2,\\
R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x)
 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
\end{split}
\]
It follows that
\[
x^2A(x,Z,R)\le Cx^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
\tag{14}
\]

The initial-modulus estimate in P2, with exponent \(\delta\), applies
to this \(z\), since \(z\ge1\) and \(f(z)=Z\le x\). It gives
\[
0\le V_f(x,z)
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}
=C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-1/a+\delta},
\tag{15}
\]
where the exponent calculation is
\[
1+\theta(2-1/d)=1+\frac{4d-2}{a}=2-\frac1a.
\tag{16}
\]
The other boundary contribution is controlled by (4), because \(x/Z\ge1\):
\[
x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}
=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}.
\tag{17}
\]
For all \(d\ge1\),
\[
\left(2-\frac1a\right)-\left(\frac12+\frac{3d}{a}\right)
=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
\tag{18}
\]
Thus (17) is at most \(C_fx^{2-1/a}\).

Here is the complete comparison of the errors in (12), (15), and
(17) with the target exponent. For \(x\ge2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{3/2+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\eta\le1/5\text{ and }\delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
xY^{1-1/d}&\le x^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-\eta},
&&\text{since }Y\le x,\ 1-1/d\ge0,\ 1/d\ge\eta,\\
x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)&\le
 C_\varepsilon x^{9/5+\varepsilon}
 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\log(2x)\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/5,\\
x^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3&\le
 C_\varepsilon x^{2-1/a+\varepsilon/2}
 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }(\log(2x))^3\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/a,\\
x^{2-1/a+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\eta\le1/a,\ \delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
x^{1/2+3d/a}&\le x^{2-1/a}\le x^{2-\eta},

# Assembly of P1–P7

Integrator's report. Inputs: `problem.md`, `plan.json`, `props/P1..P7/{statement,proof}.md`,
`results.json`. The only external text I opened was the supplied
`papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf` (J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan,
T. D. Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers*, Phil. Trans. R. Soc.
Lond. A 356 (1998) 739–761, doi:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183). I used it only to confirm
that P2 quotes Lemma 2.2 correctly; the quotation is accurate. I did not access
any excluded author, the excluded paper, GitLab, other runs or post-2010 sources.
My scripts are in `scripts/` (`constants.py`, `profile.py`).

Notation: $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, $d=\deg f$, $a=4d-1$, $\theta=2d/a$,
$\eta=\eta_d=\min\{1/5,1/a\}$, $Y=f(y)$. $W_f$, $D_f$, $R_f$, $B_f$, $K_f$, $\Theta_f$ and $F_f$
are as in P7. Their definitions in P4, P5, P6 and P7 agree verbatim; the
identifications between them are listed in §2.

## 1. Explicit composition

Fix $0<\varepsilon<\eta/2$ and put $\delta=\varepsilon/2$. Take $x\ge x_0(f)$, so that
$Z:=x^\theta\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}$ and $R:=x^{2/a}\ge 2$. Let $z\ge1$ be the
unique real number with $f(z)=Z$; it exists because $f'\ge1$.

**Case $Y\ge Z$.** Then $z\le y$, and exactly
$V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y)$.

*Step 1 (P2, first part, exponent $\delta$).* This step needs
$x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ and $Z\le Y\le x$:
$$V_f(x;z,y)=cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)+O_{f,\varepsilon}\big(x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}\big).$$

*Step 2 (P3, exponent $\delta$).* For $z<k\le y$ and $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, the
number $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$, so P3 applies to it. There are
$\le x/f(k)$ values of $h$, and $f'(k)/f(k)\ll_f 1/k$, $y\ll_f x^{1/d}$. Hence
$$S_f=M+O_{f,\varepsilon}\big(x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x\big),\qquad
M:=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{h\le x/f(k)}(x-hf(k))\,\mathfrak S(hf(k)).$$

*Step 3 (P4).* This step needs $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $Z\le Y\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$. With
$A=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}\log^2(2R)+R^{-1/2}\log^2(2R)\log(2x)$:
$$T_f=R_f\log(Y/Z)+O_f(A),\qquad M=I+O_f(x^2A),\quad I:=\int_Z^Y\sum_{h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt .$$
P4's coefficient is $\sum_r\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$. P5 shows that it equals $P_f(1)=\operatorname{Res}_{s=1}D_f$, which is the
$R_f$ of P6 and P7.

*Step 4 (P6 integral identity; needs $2\le Z\le Y\le x$).* Exactly,
$2I=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. From the definition of $F_f$, the
following identity also holds exactly:
$$x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).$$
I re-derived both identities. The $B_f$ terms cancel, and the $cx(Y-Z)$
from P2 is matched by the $c/H$ term of $F_f$.

*Steps 1–4 combined.* The errors from Step 3 are multiplied by $2$ (on $S_f$)
and by $x^2$ (on $T_f$). This gives
$$\Big|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)\Big|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}
x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x+x^2A. \tag{$*$}$$

*Step 5 (boundary terms).*
- P2, second part, at $z$: $0\le V_f(x,z)\ll_{f,\varepsilon} x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}=x^{2-1/a+\delta}$, since $1+\theta(2-1/d)=2-1/a$.
- P6, using $|F_f(H)|\ll_f H^{-3/2}$ for $H\ge1$: $x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\ll_f x^{1/2}Z^{3/2}=x^{1/2+3d/a}\le x^{2-1/a}$, because $(2-1/a)-(1/2+3d/a)=(6d-5)/(2a)>0$.

*Step 6 (bounding each error term).* With $Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}$:

| term | bound | uses |
|---|---|---|
| $x^{3/2+\delta}$ | $\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le 1/5<1/2$ |
| $xY^{1-1/d}$ | $\le x^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-\eta}$ | $Y\le x$, $\eta\le 1/a\le 1/d$ |
| $x^{9/5+\delta}\log 2x$ | $\ll_\varepsilon x^{9/5+\varepsilon}\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le1/5$ (**this is the source of the cap $1/5$**) |
| $x^2A$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a}\log^3 2x\ll_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$ | $\eta\le 1/a$ |
| $V_f(x,z)$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a+\delta}$ | $\eta\le 1/a$ |
| $x^2\lvert F_f(x/Z)\rvert$ | $\ll x^{2-1/a}$ | Step 5 |

Therefore $|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$.

**Case $Y<Z$.**
- P2, second part, at $y$: $V_f(x,y)\ll x^{1+\delta}Y^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-1/a+\delta}$.
- P6: $x^2|F_f(x/Y)|\ll x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\le x^{2-1/a}$.

The triangle inequality gives the same bound $x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}$.

**Power main term.** By P6, $|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|\le C_fH^{-13/8}$ for $H=x/Y\ge1$. Multiplying by $x^2$:
$$|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}|\le C_f\,x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}.$$
Combined with the profile estimate:
$$|V_f(x,y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}|\ll_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.$$

**Corollary in the plan.** Take $0<\delta'<\eta/3$, $x^{1-2\eta/3+\delta'}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta'}$ and $\varepsilon=\delta'$
(admissible, since $\delta'<\eta/2$). The two relative errors are:
- $x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})=(Y/x)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$;
- $x^{2-\eta+\delta'}/(x^{1/2}Y^{3/2})\le x^{-\delta'/2}\le x^{-\delta'/8}$.

Since $K_f>0$ (P5), this gives $|V_f/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\ll_{f,\delta'}x^{-\delta'/8}$ for $x\ge x_0$.

All constants depend only on $f$ and $\varepsilon$. **The propositions compose to the plan's main theorem exactly, w

... [1565 characters truncated] ...

 P6 and P7 use the Laurent definition; P5 (26) proves they agree. In any case $B_f$ cancels in the assembly.
- **$K_f$.** P5 gives $K_f=-\tfrac83\zeta(-\tfrac12)H_f(-\tfrac12)$, and P6 and P7 use $-\tfrac{16}3\operatorname{Res}_{-1/2}D_f$. They agree, because the residue of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\tfrac12$ is $\tfrac12$. ✓
- **$D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))$.** P5 states this and P6 uses it to produce the $+cH$ term. ✓
- **P5→P6 uniformity (minor, not a defect).** P5 bounds $H_f$ only on each fixed vertical line ($C(f,\sigma)$). P6 needs a bound that is uniform on the strip $-5/8\le\sigma\le2$. P6 proves this itself from the Euler product (its eq. (9)) and does not rely on P5 for it. The contour line $\Re s=-5/8$ lies inside P5's region of continuation, $\Re s>-3/4$. ✓
- **P6 ranges.** The bound $|F_f-K_fH^{-3/2}|\le CH^{-13/8}$ holds for all real $H\ge1$; P7 uses it at $H=x/Y$ and $H=x/Z$, both $\ge1$. The integral identity needs $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. ✓
- **External input.** P2 uses BGPVW Lemma 2.2 with $k=2$ and $1\le Q\le x$, which states $\Upsilon_2(x,Q)\ll x^{1+\varepsilon}Q$. I checked the PDF: the quotation is exact. P2 also correctly checks that the source's normalisation of $E$ matches ours and that all residue classes are included.

No proposition is used with a range, uniformity or error term other than the one it states. Two points are cosmetic only: the P3 dependency that is listed but unused, and the strip uniformity that P6 supplies itself rather than taking from P5.

## 3. Numerics

I recomputed the constants independently (`scripts/constants.py`), with Euler products over $p\le10^7$ plus a tail correction. The values agree with those from $p\le10^6$ to 7 digits.

| $f$ | $R_f$ | $B_f$ | $H_f(-1/2)$ | $K_f$ | `constant_extrapolated` | rel. discrepancy $(K_f-C)/C$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.3923477 | −0.4368427 | 0.2490833 | **0.1380826** | 0.134475 ± 0.007285 | **+2.68 %** (0.50 of the band) |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.3953324 | −0.4418196 | 0.2446185 | **0.1356075** | 0.136321 ± 0.002404 | **−0.52 %** (0.30 of the band) |
| $2k+1$ (extra) | 0.3786969 | −0.4242357 | 0.2572561 | 0.1426133 | 0.141686 ± 0.008218 | +0.65 % |

These match the plan's values (0.138083, 0.135608, 0.142613). None of the discrepancies is close to a clean factor.

**Diagnosing the extrapolation.** I fitted the snapshot's own model, $N(r)=C+a\sqrt r+br$, to the eight largest-$x$ ratios. I did this once on the data and once on the **exact predicted profile** $N_{\rm pred}(r)=F_f(H)H^{3/2}$ at $H=x/Y$ (`scripts/profile.py`). Intercepts:

| $f$ | fit to data | fit to predicted profile | true limit $K_f$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | 0.134475 | 0.134364 | 0.138083 |
| $k^3+2$ | 0.136321 | 0.135793 | 0.135608 |
| $2k+1$ | 0.141686 | 0.141685 | 0.142613 |

Applied to the predicted profile, the fit model reproduces the snapshot's intercepts to within 0.08 %, 0.4 % and 0.001 %. So the 2.7 % gap for $k^2+1$ is bias in the three-term model, not an error in $K_f$. The profile approaches $K_f$ slowly: at $H=200,400,700,1000$, $N_{\rm pred}$ for $k^2+1$ is 0.14024, 0.13963, 0.13891, 0.13877.

**Direct profile comparison** at $x=2.56\cdot10^8$, $(N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1)$ over the eight ratios plus the diagnostic ratio 0.005:

| $f$ | range of $N_{\rm data}/N_{\rm pred}-1$ | trend from $x=1.28\cdot10^8$ to $2.56\cdot10^8$ |
|---|---|---|
| $k^2+1$ | +0.007 % to +0.10 % | decreasing at most ratios |
| $k^3+2$ | −0.02 % to +2.2 % | decreasing at 7 of 9 ratios |
| $2k+1$ | ≤ 0.0005 % | — |

For $k^3+2$, $y$ is small (86–635), so the $k$-sampling terms (the $Z^{-1/d}$ terms in P4) are large at this $x$. The theorem's error bound $x^{2-1/11}$ is not small at $x\approx 2.6\cdot10^8$; relative to the main term it is $\approx x^{-1/11}r^{-3/2}$. The numerics are therefore consistent with the theorem but cannot test its error exponent.

## 4. Final theorem (what P1–P7 prove)

Let $f\in\mathbb Z[t]$ with $\deg f=d\ge1$, $f(t)\ge2$ and $f'(t)\ge1$ for $t\ge1$; no irreducibility or squarefreeness condition is needed. Put $Y=f(y)$ and $\eta_d=\min\{1/5,1/(4d-1)\}$. Define
$$W_f(h)=\prod_p(1-2p^{-2})\Big[1+\rho(p^{j})/(p^{j}(p^2-2))\Big],\qquad j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\},$$
and
$$\Theta_f(H)=\sum_{h\le H}W_f(h)(H-h)^2/h,\qquad F_f(H)=R_f\log H+B_f+1/(\zeta(2)H)-\Theta_f(H)/H^2,$$
where $R_f$ and $B_f$ are the residue and the shifted constant term of $D_f(s)=\sum W_f(h)h^{-s}$ at $s=1$. Let $K_f=-\tfrac83\zeta(-\tfrac12)H_f(-\tfrac12)>0$, with $H_f$ the Euler product of P5.

Then for $0<\varepsilon<\eta_d/2$, uniformly for $x\ge x_0(f,\varepsilon)$ and real $y\ge1$ with $Y\le x$:
$$V_f(x,y)=x^2F_f(x/Y)+O_{f,\varepsilon}(x^{2-\eta_d+\varepsilon}),$$
$$V_f(x,y)=K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}+O_{f,\varepsilon}(x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta_d+\varepsilon}).$$
Consequently, $V_f\sim K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$ with relative error $\ll x^{-\delta/8}$ for $x^{1-2\eta_d/3+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$.

This is exactly the plan's main theorem; there is no loss.

# Integration of the passed propositions

The propositions compose, with all errors as stated. They prove the chosen
plan's main theorem for the original polynomial class and weight, with no
additional loss. This conclusion uses the passed propositions as premises;
it does not replace their independent refereeing.

Only `problem.md`, `plan.json`, `results.json`, and the supplied proposition
artifacts were used. No external source was consulted, and no excluded source,
previous proof attempt, or previous manuscript was encountered or used.

## Common notation and coefficient interfaces

Write
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1},\quad d=\deg f,\quad Y=f(y),\quad
a=4d-1,\quad \eta=\min\{1/5,1/a\}.
\]
Use \(\mathfrak S,\lambda,W_f,D_f,P_f,H_f,\Theta_f,F_f\) exactly as
defined in P1 and P4–P6. The following identifications are essential:

* P1's \(\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)c^2G(r)^2\) is precisely the
  cube-free-supported function in P4 and P5, including \(\lambda(1)=c^2\).
* The singular series and the local factors of \(W_f\) agree in P3–P6.
  In particular, \(\rho(1)=1\) handles primes with \(p^2\mid h\).
* P5 supplies
  \[
  R_f=P_f(1)=\operatorname{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)
      =\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r.
  \]
  Thus P4's density coefficient is exactly P6's residue, rather than
  another coefficient requiring an approximation.
* Writing \(L_f\) for the constant Laurent coefficient of \(D_f\) at one,
  P5 gives \(L_f=\gamma_E R_f+P_f'(1)\); hence both definitions give
  \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\).
* At \(s=-1/2\),
  \[
  \operatorname{Res}D_f(s)=\tfrac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2),\qquad
  K_f=-\tfrac{16}{3}\operatorname{Res}D_f(s)
      =-\tfrac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.
  \]
  The factor \(1/2\) comes from \(\zeta(2s+2)\). P5 also gives
  \(D_f(0)=-c/2\), consistent with the positive \(cH\) term in P6.

## Composition before choosing the cutoffs

Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\eta/2\), and apply P2 and P3 with the smaller
exponent \(e=\varepsilon/2\). All constants below depend at most on
\(f,\varepsilon\). Initially suppose
\[
1\le z\le y,\qquad 2\le Z=f(z)\le Y\le x,\qquad 2\le R\le x.
\]
Define
\[
\begin{split}
M&=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}
             (x-hf(k))\mathfrak S(hf(k)),\\
I&=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt,\\
A&=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
      +R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x).
\end{split}
\]
The polynomial assumptions give \(f(t)\asymp_f t^d\),
\(f'(t)\ll_f t^{d-1}\), and therefore
\[
\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\ll_f\log(2x).
\]
For every pair \((k,h)\) in these sums, \(m=hf(k)\) is an integer
in \([1,x]\), as required by P3. Its error is uniform in this entire
range, including \(m\) close to \(x\). Summing that error gives
\[
\begin{split}
|S_f-M|
&\le C_e x^{4/5+e}\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\\
&\ll_{f,e}x^{9/5+e}\log(2x).
\end{split}
\]
P4 separately gives
\[
M=I+O_f(x^2A),\qquad T_f=R_f\log(Y/Z)+O_f(A).
\]
Consequently P2 implies
\[
\begin{split}
V_f(x;z,y)
={}&cx(Y-Z)+2I-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)\\
&+O_{f,e}\left(x^{3/2+e}+xY^{1-1/d}
                     +x^{9/5+e}\log(2x)+x^2A\right).
\tag{1}
\end{split}
\]
In detail, the correlation substitution contributes twice its bound;
the off-diagonal averaging contributes \(2O_f(x^2A)\), and density
averaging contributes \(-x^2O_f(A)\). These constants are absorbed in
(1); no error has been omitted.

P6's integral identity is exact:
\[
2I=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\]
The definition
\[
F_f(H)=R_f\log H+B_f+c/H-\Theta_f(H)/H^2
\]
then gives the exact cancellation
\[
\begin{split}
cx(Y-Z)+2I-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)
=x^2\{F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\}.
\end{split}
\tag{2}
\]
The \(B_f\) terms cancel, and the signs of both the logarithm and
diagonal terms agree. By P6, uniformly for \(H\ge1\),
\[
F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}+O_f(H^{-13/8}),\qquad
|F_f(H)|\ll_f H^{-3/2}.
\tag{3}
\]
Splitting the original sum at the real point \(z\), and using P2 on
the initial part, (1)–(3) now yield the full unoptimized error budget
\[
\boxed{\begin{split}
V_f(x,y)=x^2F_f(x/Y)+O_{f,e}\big(&x^{3/2+e}
 +xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5+e}\log(2x)\\
 &+x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2\\
 &+x^2R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x)\\
 &+x^{1+e}Z^{2-1/d}+x^{1/2}Z^{3/2}\big).
\end{split}}
\tag{4}
\]
The last two errors respectively dispose of \(V_f(x,z)\) and
\(x^2F_f(x/Z)\). Alternatively, expanding that boundary profile by
(3) gives a boundary main term \(K_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}\) and error
\(O_f(x^{3/8}Z^{13/8})\). The latter is bounded by the last term
of (4), since \((Z/x)^{1/8}\le1\).

## Cutoff choices and every exponent

Take
\[
\theta=\frac{2d}{4d-1}=\frac{2d}{a},\qquad
Z=x^\theta,\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(x\), depending only on \(f\),
\(Z\ge f(1)\), \(Z\ge2\), and \(R\ge2\).
Both cutoff powers are strictly less than one. Since \(f'\ge1\),
there is a unique real \(z\ge1\) with \(f(z)=Z\); if \(Y\ge Z\),
then \(z\le y\). Thus all hypotheses of P2, P4, and P6 hold.

The errors of (4) specialize as follows, retaining logarithmic losses:

| Origin | Bound after choosing the cutoffs |
|---|---|
| P2 variance reduction | \(x^{3/2+e}\) |
| P2 polynomial endpoint | \(xY^{1-1/d}\le x^{2-1/d}\) |
