\chapter{Correlations of squarefree numbers}\label{ch:correlations}

The off-diagonal term $S_f$ is a weighted sum of the correlations $C_x(m)$ of \eqref{eq:Cx}. We need an asymptotic formula for $C_x(m)$ that is uniform in the whole range $1\le m\le x$, including differences $m$ close to $x$, where the number $x-m$ of available pairs is small. Counts of pairs of squarefree numbers with a given difference have a long history (see for example \cite{mirsky1949}, and the discussion of the related binary additive problem in \cite[\S1]{bgpvw1998}). The archived proof gives a self-contained elementary argument with an explicit absolute constant. The archived plan anticipated a circle-method argument based on \cite{bgpvw1998}, but the proof does not need it. (Archived source: proposition P3.)

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:corr}
There is an absolute constant $K_{\mathrm c}$ such that for all real $x\ge2$ and all integers $1\le m\le x$,
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\Sing(m)\bigr|\le K_{\mathrm c}\,x^{4/5}.
\]
One may take $K_{\mathrm c}=67+2D_{1/10}$, with $D_{1/10}$ as in \cref{lem:divisor}. In particular, for every $\eps>0$ the bound $C(\eps)x^{4/5+\eps}$ holds, which is the form recorded in the archived plan.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $L=x-m\ge0$ and $H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor$, so that $\frac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}$ and $H\ge1$. All bounds below hold for every real $L\ge0$, including $L<1$, when $C_x(m)=0$.

\emph{Truncation.} For $k\ge1$ split \eqref{eq:mu2} as $\mu^2(k)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)$, where
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e\le H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e),\qquad R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e>H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e).
\]
Then $|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k)$ and $|R_H(k)|\le\#\{e>H:e^2\mid k\}$. Each of the sets $\{n:1\le n\le L\}$ and $\{n+m:1\le n\le L\}$ consists of integers in $[1,x]$, because $m+L=x$. Each contains at most $x/e^2$ multiples of $e^2$. Therefore, by \cref{lem:sums}(a),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RH-sum}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n)|\le\sum_{e>H}\frac x{e^2}\le\frac xH,\qquad\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n+m)|\le\frac xH.
\end{equation}
The exact identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
together with $0\le\mu^2\le1$ and $|T_H(n)|\le\tau(n)\le D_{1/10}x^{1/10}$ (\cref{lem:divisor}) bounds each summand by $|R_H(n)|+D_{1/10}x^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|$. Summing with \eqref{eq:RH-sum},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-trunc}
\Bigl|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\Bigr|\le(1+D_{1/10}x^{1/10})\frac xH\le2x^{3/5}+2D_{1/10}x^{7/10}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Counting the truncated congruences.} Let $e_1,e_2\le H$ and $g=(e_1,e_2)$. The congruences $n\equiv0\bmod e_1^2$ and $n\equiv-m\bmod e_2^2$ are soluble exactly when $g^2\mid m$. Necessity follows by reducing modulo $g^2$. For sufficiency write $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ with $(a,b)=1$ and $n=e_1^2u$; the second congruence becomes $a^2u\equiv-m/g^2\bmod b^2$, which determines $u$ modulo $b^2$. Hence the solutions form one residue class modulo $e_1^2e_2^2/g^2$. For any residue class modulo $h$ with representative $r$, the number of its members in $[1,L]$ is $\lfloor(L-r)/h\rfloor-\lfloor-r/h\rfloor=L/h+\theta$ with $|\theta|\le1$. Expanding both truncated sums therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-AH}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=L\,\mathcal A_H(m)+E_H,\qquad|E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5},
\end{equation}
where
\[
\mathcal A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{e_1,e_2\le H\\(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m}}\frac{\mu(e_1)\mu(e_2)(e_1,e_2)^2}{e_1^2e_2^2}.
\]

\emph{Completing the series.} Let $\mathcal A(m)$ denote the same sum over all $e_1,e_2\ge1$. Writing $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ and dropping the coprimality of $a,b$ shows absolute convergence:
$\sum_{e_1,e_2}(e_1,e_2)^2/(e_1e_2)^2\le\sum_gg^{-2}\sum_aa^{-2}\sum_bb^{-2}\le8$. For the tail with $e_1>H$, the same substitution gives the bound $\sum_gg^{-2}\bigl(\sum_{a>H/g}a^{-2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_bb^{-2}\bigr)$. For $g\le H$ the summand is at most $g^{-2}(2g/H)\cdot2=4/(gH)$ by \cref{lem:sums}(a), and summing over $g\le H$ gives at most $4(1+\log H)/H$. For $g>H$ the summand is at most $4/g^2$, and these sum to at most $4/H$. By symmetry the tail with $e_2>H$ has the same bound, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-tail}
|\mathcal A(m)-\mathcal A_H(m)|\le\frac{8(2+\log H)}H,
\end{equation}
uniformly in $m$, because the condition $(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m$ was dropped.

\emph{The Euler product.} By absolute convergence, $\mathcal A(m)$ factors over primes, the argument of \cref{lem:euler} applying verbatim to the double sum. Only the exponents $0$ and $1$ occur in $e_1,e_2$. At a prime $p$ the four choices contribute $1$, $-p^{-2}$, $-p^{-2}$, and $p^{-2}\one_{p^2\mid m}$, so by \eqref{eq:sing}
\[
\mathcal A(m)=\prod_p\Bigl(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\one_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\Bigr)=\Sing(m).
\]

\emph{Conclusion.} Since $0\le L\le x$, $H\ge\frac12x^{2/5}$ and $\log H\le\frac25\log x\le2x^{1/5}$ (\cref{lem:sums}(d)), \eqref{eq:corr-tail} gives
\[
L\,|\mathcal A_H(m)-\Sing(m)|\le16x^{3/5}\bigl(2+\tfrac25\log x\bigr)\le32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\]
Combining with \eqref{eq:corr-trunc} and \eqref{eq:corr-AH} gives $|C_x(m)-L\Sing(m)|\le(2+2D_{1/10}+1+64)x^{4/5}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The constant $D_{1/10}$ is astronomically large, but only its existence matters. For the application in \cref{ch:assembly} only the exponent $4/5$ is relevant: summing the error over the roughly $x\log x$ weighted pairs $(h,k)$ costs $x^{9/5+\eps}$, and this caps the saving in \cref{thm:main} at $\eta_d\le1/5$.
\end{remark}

1	\chapter{Averaging over polynomial moduli}\label{ch:averaging}
2	
3	After \cref{ch:variance,ch:correlations} the variance is expressed through two sums over $k$: the density term $T_f(z,y)$ and the main part of the off-diagonal term,
4	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mf}
5	M_f(x;z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}\bigl(x-hf(k)\bigr)\Sing\bigl(hf(k)\bigr).
6	\end{equation}
7	Both involve arithmetic functions of $f(k)$. Expanding them over $r$ with the coefficients $\lambda(r)$ of \cref{ch:densities} makes the dependence on $k$ periodic modulo $r$. Partial summation then replaces the sum over $k$ by an integral in the variable $t=f(k)$, with $f'(k)$ acting as the Jacobian. This is the role of the weight $f'(k)$. (Archived source: proposition P4, a crux of the plan.)
8	
9	\section{The averaged singular series}
10	
11	For $h\ge1$ and a prime $p$ put
12	\[
13	\delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:\ p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
14	\]
15	If $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$, then $p^2\mid hf(a)$ is equivalent to $p^j\mid f(a)$. Counting lifts from residues modulo $p^j$ to residues modulo $p^2$ gives
16	\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltap}
17	\delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^{j})}{p^{j}}\in[0,1],\qquad\text{so}\qquad
18	1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
19	\end{equation}
20	where $w_p(h)$ is the local factor in \eqref{eq:W-intro}. Comparing with the second form of \eqref{eq:sing}, $W_f(h)=\prod_pw_p(h)$ is what one obtains by replacing the indicator $\one_{p^2\mid hf(k)}$ in $\Sing(hf(k))$ by its average $\delta_p(h)$ over $k$. \Cref{lem:W-ident} below makes this precise.
21	
22	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-basic}
23	For every $h\ge1$ and prime $p$, $1-2p^{-2}\le w_p(h)\le1-p^{-2}$. Hence the product $W_f(h)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $h$, and $0<W_f(h)\le1$. The series
24	\[
25	\widetilde R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
26	\]
27	converges absolutely and $0\le\widetilde R_f\le c$.
28	\end{lemma}
29	
30	\begin{proof}
31	The bounds for $w_p$ follow from $\delta_p(h)\in[0,1]$, so $|w_p(h)-1|\le2p^{-2}$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. The factors are positive, so $W_f(h)>0$, and they are at most one. Finally $0\le\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
32	\end{proof}
33	
34	For $r,h\ge1$ define
35	\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
36	\beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r\frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)},
37	\end{equation}
38	the mean value of the $r$-periodic sequence
39	\[
40	k\longmapsto\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
41	\]
42	Note $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ by \cref{lem:ramanujan}(b).
43	
44	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-ident}
45	For every $h\ge1$, $\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=W_f(h)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly in $h$.
46	\end{lemma}
47	
48	\begin{proof}
49	Absolute and uniform convergence follow from $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$. If $(r,s)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies $a\bmod rs$ with pairs $(a\bmod r,\ a\bmod s)$. Moreover $c_{rs}=c_rc_s$, $c_r(hf(a))$ depends only on $a\bmod r$, and $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$. Hence $\beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)$. Thus $\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)$ is $c^2$ times a multiplicative function supported on cube-free $r$, and \cref{lem:euler} gives
50	\[
51	\sum_r\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=c^2\prod_p\Bigl(1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)
52	\]
53	by \eqref{eq:lambda-p}. The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ may equally be taken over $a\bmod p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:cp-sum},
54	\[
55	(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)=\frac1{p^2}\sum_{a\bmod p^2}\bigl(c_p+c_{p^2}\bigr)(hf(a))=p^2\delta_p(h)-1.
56	\]
57	Distributing $c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2$ over the primes, the local factor becomes
58	\[
59	\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2+p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{p^4}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
60	\]
61	by \eqref{eq:deltap}. No restriction on $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
62	\end{proof}
63	
64	\section{A partial summation lemma}
65	
66	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:periodic}
67	Let $b$ be a periodic sequence with integer period $r\ge1$, $|b(k)|\le1$, and mean $m_b=r^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^rb(a)$. Let $1\le u\le v$ be real and let $F$ be continuously differentiable on $[u,v]$. Then
68	\[
69	\Bigl|\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t\Bigr|\le4r\Bigl(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\dd t\Bigr).
70	\]
71	\end{lemma}
72	
73	\begin{proof}
74	Let $P(t)=\sum_{k\le t}b(k)-m_bt$. Writing $t=qr+s$ with $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\le s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel, the remaining at most $r$ terms have modulus at most $1$, and $|m_bs|\le r$; so $|P(t)|\le2r$. Hence $D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\le t}b(k)-m_b(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)$ satisfies $|D_u(t)|\le4r$ and $D_u(u)=0$. Riemann--Stieltjes integration by parts gives the identity
75	\[
76	\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t=\int_u^vF(t)\dd D_u(t)=F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\dd t,
77	\]
78	from which the bound follows.
79	\end{proof}
80	
81	With $F=w=f'/f$ on $[z,y]$, \cref{lem:poly}(b) gives $|w(y)|\le U/y\le U/z$ and $\int_z^y|w'|\le V/z$. Since $\int_z^yw=\log(Y/Z)$, we obtain for every $r$-periodic $b$ as in \cref{lem:periodic} and $1\le z\le y$:
82	\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic-w}
83	\Bigl|\sum_{z<k\le y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}-m_b\log\frac YZ\Bigr|\le\frac{4D_wr}z,\qquad D_w=U+V.
84	\end{equation}
85	
86	\section{The averaging proposition}
87	
88	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:averaging}
89	There is $C(f)>0$ such that the following holds uniformly for real $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ with $Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$, and real $2\le R\le x$. With
90	\[
91	\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)
92	\]
93	and
94	\begin{equation}\label{eq:If}
95	I_f(x;Z,Y)=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t,
96	\end{equation}
97	we have
98	\begin{align}
99	\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,\mathcal A,\label{eq:avg1}\\
100	\bigl|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,x^2\mathcal A.\label{eq:avg2}
101	\end{align}
102	No condition on the discriminant, content or factorisation of $f$ is imposed.
103	\end{proposition}
104	
105	Throughout the proof, $\mathcal T(R)$ and $\mathcal N(R)$ are as in \cref{prop:second-moment}(d), so that $\mathcal T(R)\le C_0R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2$ and $\mathcal N(R)\le C_0R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2$. If $z=y$ both assertions are trivial, so we assume $z<y$.
106	
107	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg1}]
108	By \cref{prop:second-moment}(a) applied to $q=f(k)$,
109	\[
110	T_f(z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
111	\]
112	The part with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most $\mathcal T(R)\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)/f(k)\le2U\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$ by \eqref{eq:sum-w}. For each $r\le R$, the sequence $b(k)=\one_{r\mid f(k)}$ has period $r$ and mean $\rho(r)/r$, so \eqref{eq:periodic-w} gives
113	\[
114	\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\one_{r\mid f(k)}=\frac{\rho(r)}r\log\frac YZ+e_r,\qquad|e_r|\le\frac{4D_wr}z.
115	\]
116	Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ produces an error at most $4D_w\mathcal N(R)/z$. Completing $\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$ to $\widetilde R_f$ costs at most $\mathcal T(R)\log(Y/Z)\le\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$, because $\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. Since $Z\le\kappa_2z^d$, we have $z^{-1}\le\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}$, and therefore
117	\[
118	\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|\le C_0\Bigl(4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).\qedhere
119	\]
120	\end{proof}
121	
122	For the second assertion we first need a bound for the weight functions. Let $H_0=\lfloor x/Z\rfloor$. For $1\le h\le H_0$ define
123	\[
124	v_h=\min\{y,\,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad F_h(t)=f'(t)\bigl(x-hf(t)\bigr)\quad(z\le t\le v_h),
125	\]
126	which is legitimate because $x/h\ge Z=f(z)$ (\cref{lem:poly}(a)). Then $z\le v_h\le(x/(\kappa_1h))^{1/d}$ and $0\le x-hf(t)\le x$ on $[z,v_h]$. Put
127	\[
128	K_2=\begin{cases}\kappa_2+\kappa_2^2/\kappa_1,&d=1,\\ \kappa_2+\kappa_2/(d-1)+\kappa_2^2/((2d-1)\kappa_1),&d\ge2.\end{cases}
129	\]
130	
131	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:weight-var}
132	For $1\le h\le H_0$, $\displaystyle|F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\dd t\le K_2\,x\,v_h^{d-1}$.
133	\end{lemma}
134	
135	\begin{proof}
136	We have $|F_h(v_h)|\le\kappa_2xv_h^{d-1}$ and $|F_h'|\le|f''|(x-hf)+hf'^2$. For $d\ge2$,
137	\[
138	\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le\kappa_2x\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\dd t+h\kappa_2^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\dd t\le\frac{\kappa_2}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}+\frac{h\kappa_2^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1},
139	\]
140	and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
141	\end{proof}
142	
143	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
144	\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
145	\[
146	\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
147	\]
148	By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
149	\[
150	|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
151	\]
152	uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
153	\[
154	|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
155	\]
156	Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.
157	
158	\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
159	\[
160	M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
161	\]
162	The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
163	\[
164	\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
165	\]
166	and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
167	\[
168	|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
169	\]
170	
171	Combining the three estimates proves
172	\[
173	|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
174	\]
175	Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
176	\end{proof}
177	
178	\begin{remark}
179	The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
180	\end{remark}

\chapter{Averaging over polynomial moduli}\label{ch:averaging}

After \cref{ch:variance,ch:correlations} the variance is expressed through two sums over $k$: the density term $T_f(z,y)$ and the main part of the off-diagonal term,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mf}
M_f(x;z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}\bigl(x-hf(k)\bigr)\Sing\bigl(hf(k)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both involve arithmetic functions of $f(k)$. Expanding them over $r$ with the coefficients $\lambda(r)$ of \cref{ch:densities} makes the dependence on $k$ periodic modulo $r$. Partial summation then replaces the sum over $k$ by an integral in the variable $t=f(k)$, with $f'(k)$ acting as the Jacobian. This is the role of the weight $f'(k)$. (Archived source: proposition P4, a crux of the plan.)

\section{The averaged singular series}

For $h\ge1$ and a prime $p$ put
\[
\delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:\ p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
If $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$, then $p^2\mid hf(a)$ is equivalent to $p^j\mid f(a)$. Counting lifts from residues modulo $p^j$ to residues modulo $p^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltap}
\delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^{j})}{p^{j}}\in[0,1],\qquad\text{so}\qquad
1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\end{equation}
where $w_p(h)$ is the local factor in \eqref{eq:W-intro}. Comparing with the second form of \eqref{eq:sing}, $W_f(h)=\prod_pw_p(h)$ is what one obtains by replacing the indicator $\one_{p^2\mid hf(k)}$ in $\Sing(hf(k))$ by its average $\delta_p(h)$ over $k$. \Cref{lem:W-ident} below makes this precise.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-basic}
For every $h\ge1$ and prime $p$, $1-2p^{-2}\le w_p(h)\le1-p^{-2}$. Hence the product $W_f(h)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $h$, and $0<W_f(h)\le1$. The series
\[
\widetilde R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
\]
converges absolutely and $0\le\widetilde R_f\le c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The bounds for $w_p$ follow from $\delta_p(h)\in[0,1]$, so $|w_p(h)-1|\le2p^{-2}$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. The factors are positive, so $W_f(h)>0$, and they are at most one. Finally $0\le\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
\end{proof}

For $r,h\ge1$ define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
\beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r\frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)},
\end{equation}
the mean value of the $r$-periodic sequence
\[
k\longmapsto\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
Note $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ by \cref{lem:ramanujan}(b).

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-ident}
For every $h\ge1$, $\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=W_f(h)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly in $h$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Absolute and uniform convergence follow from $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$. If $(r,s)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies $a\bmod rs$ with pairs $(a\bmod r,\ a\bmod s)$. Moreover $c_{rs}=c_rc_s$, $c_r(hf(a))$ depends only on $a\bmod r$, and $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$. Hence $\beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)$. Thus $\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)$ is $c^2$ times a multiplicative function supported on cube-free $r$, and \cref{lem:euler} gives
\[
\sum_r\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=c^2\prod_p\Bigl(1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)
\]
by \eqref{eq:lambda-p}. The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ may equally be taken over $a\bmod p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:cp-sum},
\[
(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)=\frac1{p^2}\sum_{a\bmod p^2}\bigl(c_p+c_{p^2}\bigr)(hf(a))=p^2\delta_p(h)-1.
\]
Distributing $c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2$ over the primes, the local factor becomes
\[
\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2+p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{p^4}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\]
by \eqref{eq:deltap}. No restriction on $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
\end{proof}

\section{A partial summation lemma}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:periodic}
Let $b$ be a periodic sequence with integer period $r\ge1$, $|b(k)|\le1$, and mean $m_b=r^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^rb(a)$. Let $1\le u\le v$ be real and let $F$ be continuously differentiable on $[u,v]$. Then
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t\Bigr|\le4r\Bigl(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\dd t\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $P(t)=\sum_{k\le t}b(k)-m_bt$. Writing $t=qr+s$ with $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\le s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel, the remaining at most $r$ terms have modulus at most $1$, and $|m_bs|\le r$; so $|P(t)|\le2r$. Hence $D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\le t}b(k)-m_b(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)$ satisfies $|D_u(t)|\le4r$ and $D_u(u)=0$. Riemann--Stieltjes integration by parts gives the identity
\[
\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t=\int_u^vF(t)\dd D_u(t)=F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\dd t,
\]
from which the bound follows.
\end{proof}

With $F=w=f'/f$ on $[z,y]$, \cref{lem:poly}(b) gives $|w(y)|\le U/y\le U/z$ and $\int_z^y|w'|\le V/z$. Since $\int_z^yw=\log(Y/Z)$, we obtain for every $r$-periodic $b$ as in \cref{lem:periodic} and $1\le z\le y$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic-w}
\Bigl|\sum_{z<k\le y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}-m_b\log\frac YZ\Bigr|\le\frac{4D_wr}z,\qquad D_w=U+V.
\end{equation}

\section{The averaging proposition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:averaging}
There is $C(f)>0$ such that the following holds uniformly for real $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ with $Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$, and real $2\le R\le x$. With
\[
\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:If}
I_f(x;Z,Y)=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t,
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{align}
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,\mathcal A,\label{eq:avg1}\\
\bigl|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,x^2\mathcal A.\label{eq:avg2}
\end{align}
No condition on the discriminant, content or factorisation of $f$ is imposed.
\end{proposition}

Throughout the proof, $\mathcal T(R)$ and $\mathcal N(R)$ are as in \cref{prop:second-moment}(d), so that $\mathcal T(R)\le C_0R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2$ and $\mathcal N(R)\le C_0R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2$. If $z=y$ both assertions are trivial, so we assume $z<y$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg1}]
By \cref{prop:second-moment}(a) applied to $q=f(k)$,
\[
T_f(z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
\]
The part with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most $\mathcal T(R)\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)/f(k)\le2U\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$ by \eqref{eq:sum-w}. For each $r\le R$, the sequence $b(k)=\one_{r\mid f(k)}$ has period $r$ and mean $\rho(r)/r$, so \eqref{eq:periodic-w} gives
\[
\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\one_{r\mid f(k)}=\frac{\rho(r)}r\log\frac YZ+e_r,\qquad|e_r|\le\frac{4D_wr}z.
\]
Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ produces an error at most $4D_w\mathcal N(R)/z$. Completing $\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$ to $\widetilde R_f$ costs at most $\mathcal T(R)\log(Y/Z)\le\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$, because $\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. Since $Z\le\kappa_2z^d$, we have $z^{-1}\le\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}$, and therefore
\[
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|\le C_0\Bigl(4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

For the second assertion we first need a bound for the weight functions. Let $H_0=\lfloor x/Z\rfloor$. For $1\le h\le H_0$ define
\[
v_h=\min\{y,\,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad F_h(t)=f'(t)\bigl(x-hf(t)\bigr)\quad(z\le t\le v_h),
\]
which is legitimate because $x/h\ge Z=f(z)$ (\cref{lem:poly}(a)). Then $z\le v_h\le(x/(\kappa_1h))^{1/d}$ and $0\le x-hf(t)\le x$ on $[z,v_h]$. Put
\[
K_2=\begin{cases}\kappa_2+\kappa_2^2/\kappa_1,&d=1,\\ \kappa_2+\kappa_2/(d-1)+\kappa_2^2/((2d-1)\kappa_1),&d\ge2.\end{cases}
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:weight-var}
For $1\le h\le H_0$, $\displaystyle|F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\dd t\le K_2\,x\,v_h^{d-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have $|F_h(v_h)|\le\kappa_2xv_h^{d-1}$ and $|F_h'|\le|f''|(x-hf)+hf'^2$. For $d\ge2$,
\[
\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le\kappa_2x\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\dd t+h\kappa_2^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\dd t\le\frac{\kappa_2}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}+\frac{h\kappa_2^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1},
\]
and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
\[
\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
\[
|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
\]
uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
\[
|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
\]
Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.

\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
\[
M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
\[
\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
\]
and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
\[
|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
\]

Combining the three estimates proves
\[
|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
\]
Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
\end{remark}

1	\chapter{The Dirichlet series of the averaged singular series}\label{ch:dirichlet}
2	
3	The averaged singular series $W_f(h)$ is a product of local factors that depend only on whether $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. Its Dirichlet series therefore factors as $\zeta(s)$ times an Euler product, and a second factorisation exhibits a pole of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\frac12$. This pole, which is invisible in the region of absolute convergence, produces the main term of \cref{thm:main}. (Archived source: proposition P5, a crux of the plan.)
4	
5	\section{Facts about the zeta function}
6	
7	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta}
8	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
9	\item For every integer $N\ge1$ and $\re w>0$, $w\ne1$,
10	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-N}
11	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}-w\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-w-1}\dd u.
12	\end{equation}
13	In $\re w>0$ the only pole of $\zeta$ is a simple pole at $w=1$ with residue $1$, and $\lim_{w\to1}\bigl(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\bigr)=\gamma_E$, Euler's constant.
14	\item Let $\mathcal B_2(u)=\{u\}^2-\{u\}+\frac16$. The formula
15	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-B2}
16	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}-\frac{w(w+1)}2\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u
17	\end{equation}
18	continues $\zeta$ meromorphically to $\re w>-1$, with the single pole at $w=1$. In particular $\zeta(0)=-\frac12$ and $-\frac14\le\zeta(-\frac12)\le-\frac16$.
19	\end{enumerate}
20	\end{lemma}
21	
22	\begin{proof}
23	(a) For $\re w>1$ write $\sum_{n>N}n^{-w}=\int_N^\infty u^{-w}\dd\lfloor u\rfloor$, replace $\lfloor u\rfloor=u-\{u\}$, and integrate the second part by parts; the boundary term at $N$ vanishes because $\{N\}=0$. This gives \eqref{eq:zeta-N}. The integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $\re w>0$ because $0\le\{u\}<1$, which gives the continuation and the description of the pole. Subtracting $1/(w-1)$ and letting $w\to1$ gives $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N-\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-2}\dd u$. The integral lies in $[0,1/N]$, and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\gamma_E$ by its definition as $\lim(\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N)$.
24	
25	(b) With $N=1$, \eqref{eq:zeta-N} becomes $\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12-w\int_1^\infty(\{u\}-\frac12)u^{-w-1}\dd u$. The function $\mathcal B_2$ is continuous, satisfies $|\mathcal B_2|\le\frac16$, and has derivative $2(\{u\}-\frac12)$ between integers. Integration by parts over $[1,T]$ for integers $T\ge2$ gives
26	\[
27	\int_1^T\Bigl(\{u\}-\frac12\Bigr)u^{-w-1}\dd u=\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}+\frac{w+1}2\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u,
28	\]
29	and letting $T\to\infty$ for $\re w>1$ yields \eqref{eq:zeta-B2}. The last integral and its $w$-derivatives are dominated on $\re w\ge\eta>-1$ by $(\log u)^mu^{-\eta-2}/6$, so the integral is holomorphic for $\re w>-1$. At $w=0$ the formula gives $-1+\frac12=-\frac12$. At $w=-\frac12$ it gives $\zeta(-\frac12)=-\frac5{24}+\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-3/2}\dd u$, and the integral has modulus at most $\frac16\cdot2=\frac13$.
30	\end{proof}

32	\section{The local factors}
33	
34	For each prime $p$ put
35	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd}
36	\alpha_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
37	\beta_p=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
38	\delta_p=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
39	\end{equation}
40	By \eqref{eq:W-intro}, $w_p(h)$ equals $\alpha_p$, $\alpha_p+\beta_p$ or $\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p$ according as $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. By \cref{lem:rho} (with $C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|\}$),
41	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd-bounds}
42	1-\frac2{p^2}\le\alpha_p\le1,\quad0\le\beta_p\le\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}\le\frac{C_0}{p^3},\quad0\le\delta_p\le\frac1{p^2},\quad\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-\frac1{p^2}.
43	\end{equation}
44	Here $\beta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)$, $\delta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p)\le p$, and $\alpha_p\le1$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p^2$. Define
45	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LM}
46	L_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s},\qquad
47	M_p(s)=\bigl(1-p^{-2s-2}\bigr)L_p(s),
48	\end{equation}
49	and $P_f(s)=\prod_pL_p(s)$, $H_f(s)=\prod_pM_p(s)$. In the notation of the archived proposition, $L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})B_p(s)$ with $B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p-a_p)p^{-s}+(c_p-b_p)p^{-2s}$, $a_p=1+\rho(p^2)/(p^2(p^2-2))$, $b_p=1+\rho(p)/(p(p^2-2))$, $c_p=1+1/(p^2-2)$. Expanding the product, with $z=p^{-s}$,
50	\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-expand}
51	M_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\bigl(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}\bigr)z^2-\beta_pp^{-2}z^3-\delta_pp^{-2}z^4,\qquad
52	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}=-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6}.
53	\end{equation}
54	The cancellation of the terms $\pm p^{-2}$ in the coefficient of $z^2$ is what allows $H_f$ to converge beyond $\re s=-\frac12$.

57	
58	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Df}
59	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
60	\item The series $D_f(s)=\sum_hW_f(h)h^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\re s>1$.
61	\item The products $P_f$ and $H_f$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, and define holomorphic functions, on $\re s>-\frac12$ and $\re s>-\frac34$ respectively. For every fixed $\sigma>-\frac34$ there is $C(f,\sigma)$ with $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le C(f,\sigma)$ for all real $t$.
62	\item For $\re s>1$, $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. The function $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ continues $D_f$ meromorphically to $\re s>-\frac34$, and its only possible poles there are simple poles at $s=1$ and $s=-\frac12$.
63	\item $R_f=\Res_{s=1}D_f(s)=P_f(1)$. Moreover $R_f=\widetilde R_f$, where $\widetilde R_f$ is the series of \cref{lem:W-basic}, and \eqref{eq:R-intro} holds. Moreover $B_f=(\gamma_E-\frac32)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and $R_f>0$.
64	\item $D_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}=-\frac c2$.
65	\item We have $\Res_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)=\frac12\zeta(-\frac12)H_f(-\frac12)$, and hence
66	\[
67	K_f=-\tfrac83\,\zeta(-\tfrac12)\,H_f(-\tfrac12).
68	\]
69	Moreover $H_f(-\frac12)>0$ and $K_f>0$, and $K_f$ is given by the absolutely convergent product \eqref{eq:K-intro}.
70	\end{enumerate}
71	\end{proposition}
72	
73	\begin{proof}
74	(a) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $0<W_f(h)\le1$, so $\sum_h|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_hh^{-\re s}$.
75	
76	(b) For $\re s\ge\sigma$, \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} gives $|L_p(s)-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}$. If $\sigma>-\frac12$ all exponents exceed one, so by \cref{lem:sums}(c) the sum over $p$ converges uniformly on $\re s\ge\sigma$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. For $M_p$, \eqref{eq:M-expand} and \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} give, for $\re s\ge\sigma$,
77	\[
78	|M_p(s)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}+\frac{C_0}{p^{3+\sigma}}+\Bigl(\frac{C_0}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}+\frac{C_0}{p^5}\Bigr)p^{-2\sigma}+\frac{C_0}{p^{5+3\sigma}}+\frac1{p^{4+4\sigma}}.
79	\]
80	For $\sigma>-\frac34$ the exponents $2$, $3+\sigma$, $3+2\sigma$, $4+2\sigma$, $5+2\sigma$, $5+3\sigma$ and $4+4\sigma$ all exceed one. Hence $\sum_p\sup_{\re s\ge\sigma}|M_p(s)-1|=:E_H(\sigma)<\infty$, and \cref{lem:products} gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, holomorphy, and $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(E_H(\sigma))$ for all $t$.
81	
82	(c) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p>0$, and $u(h)=W_f(h)/W_f(1)$ is multiplicative with $u(p)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p)/\alpha_p$ and $u(p^e)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p)/\alpha_p$ for $e\ge2$. For $\re s>1$ and $z=p^{-s}$ its local series is
83	\[
84	1+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p}{\alpha_p}z+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p}{\alpha_p}\cdot\frac{z^2}{1-z}=\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\delta_pz^2}{\alpha_p(1-z)}=\frac{L_p(s)}{\alpha_p(1-p^{-s})}.
85	\]
86	Since $\sum_h|u(h)h^{-s}|<\infty$, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\sum_hu(h)h^{-s}=\prod_pL_p(s)\alpha_p^{-1}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. Multiplying by the convergent product $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p$ and using the Euler product of $\zeta$ gives $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)$; the limits of partial products multiply. For $\re s>-\frac12$ we have $\re(2s+2)>1$, so $\prod_p(1-p^{-2s-2})^{-1}=\zeta(2s+2)$ converges absolutely, and multiplying the products gives $P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. By \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(2s+2)$ are meromorphic for $\re s>-\frac34$, since then $\re s>-1$ and $\re(2s+2)>\frac12$. Their only poles there are at $s=1$ and at $2s+2=1$, both simple. Since $H_f$ is holomorphic, $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ is the required continuation.
87	
88	(d) Since $P_f$ is holomorphic near $1$ and $\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1)$ by \cref{lem:zeta}(a), we have $D_f(s)=\frac{P_f(1)}{s-1}+\gamma_EP_f(1)+P_f'(1)+O(s-1)$. This gives $R_f=P_f(1)$ and the formula for $B_f$ from \eqref{eq:RBK}. Substituting \eqref{eq:abd},
89	\[
90	L_p(1)=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}p+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}
91	=\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\bigl(1+T_p\bigr),
92	\]
93	with $T_p=(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))/(p^2-1)^2\ge0$. By \cref{lem:rho}(d) and $p^2-1\ge\frac34p^2$, $T_p\le\frac{16C_0}9(p^{-3}+p^{-4})$, which is summable. Using \eqref{eq:c-euler}, $R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p(1+T_p)>0$, which is \eqref{eq:R-intro}. For the identification with $\widetilde R_f$, note that $\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=c^2v(r)$, where $v$ is the nonnegative multiplicative function supported on cube-free integers with
94	\[
95	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad v(p^2)=\frac{\varphi(p^2)\rho(p^2)}{p^2(p^2-1)^2}=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2},
96	\]
97	using \cref{lem:rho}(a) for multiplicativity of $\rho$. Thus $1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p$. Since $\sum_rv(r)<\infty$ by \cref{lem:W-basic}, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\widetilde R_f=c^2\prod_p(1+T_p)=R_f$.
98	
99	(e) $L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}$, so $P_f(0)=c$ by \eqref{eq:c-euler}. The identity $D_f=\zeta P_f$ persists on $\re s>-\frac12$ by (c), and both factors are regular at $0$; by \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $D_f(0)=\zeta(0)c=-c/2$.
100	
101	(f) Near $s=-\frac12$, $\zeta(2s+2)=\frac{1/2}{s+1/2}+O(1)$, while $\zeta(s)$ and $H_f(s)$ are holomorphic. This gives the residue, and the formula for $K_f$ follows from \eqref{eq:RBK}. At $s=-\frac12$,
102	\[
103	M_p(-\tfrac12)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\Bigl(1+\frac1p-\frac{2+\rho(p)}{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p)}{p^{5/2}}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^{7/2}}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4}\Bigr),
104	\]
105	by direct substitution of \eqref{eq:abd}. This is positive because $\alpha_p>0$ and $\beta_p,\delta_p\ge0$. The deviations $|M_p(-\frac12)-1|$ are summable by (b), so \cref{lem:products}(c) gives $H_f(-\frac12)>0$, and \cref{lem:zeta}(b) gives $\zeta(-\frac12)<0$. Hence $K_f>0$, and \eqref{eq:K-intro} is the product $H_f(-\frac12)=\prod_pM_p(-\frac12)$, with the factors at each prime kept together.
106	\end{proof}
107	
108	\begin{remark}
109	Both poles in (c) are genuine, since $R_f>0$ and $K_f>0$. The value $D_f(0)=-c/2$ is essential: in \cref{ch:mellin} it produces the term $+cH$ in the expansion of $\Theta_f(H)$, which cancels the diagonal term $cx(Y-Z)$ of \cref{prop:reduction}. The identity $R_f=\widetilde R_f$ makes the logarithmic terms cancel as well.
110	\end{remark}

11	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:interval}
12	Let $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$, and let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)$ be as in \cref{prop:averaging}. Then
13	\[
14	\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A\bigr).
15	\]
16	\end{lemma}
17	
18	\begin{proof}
19	\emph{Correlations.} For $z<k\le y$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ integers $h$ with $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, and each $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$. By \cref{prop:corr}, replacing $C_x(m)$ by $(x-m)\Sing(m)$ costs at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{4/5}$ for each pair $(h,k)$. After multiplying by $f'(k)$ and summing over $h$, the cost is at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}f'(k)/f(k)$, and by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
20	\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-M}
21	|S_f(x;z,y)-M_f(x;z,y)|\le2UK_{\mathrm c}\,x^{9/5}\log(2x).
22	\end{equation}
23	\emph{Averaging.} \Cref{prop:averaging} applies under exactly the present hypotheses and gives
24	\[
25	|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2\mathcal A,\qquad|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_f\mathcal A,
26	\]
27	where we used $\widetilde R_f=R_f$ (\cref{prop:Df}(d)).
28	
29	\emph{Combination.} By \cref{prop:reduction}, the factor $2$ in front of $S_f$ and the factor $x^2$ in front of $T_f$ give
30	\begin{multline*}
31	\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-\bigl[cx(Y-Z)+2I_f(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr]\Bigr|\\
32	\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}\bigr)+4UK_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}\log(2x)+3C_fx^2\mathcal A.
33	\end{multline*}
34	\emph{Exact cancellation.} By \cref{lem:integral-identity}, $2I_f(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. By the definition \eqref{eq:ThetaF} of $F_f$, with $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, direct subtraction gives
35	\[
36	x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y),
37	\]
38	because $x^2\cdot c/(x/Y)=cxY$ and the $B_f$-terms cancel. Hence the bracket equals $x^2(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z))$.
39	\end{proof}

112	\section{Where the exponents come from}
113	
114	The cap $\eta_d\le\frac15$ comes from summing the uniform correlation error $x^{4/5}$ of \cref{prop:corr} over all pairs $(h,k)$; the weighted number of these pairs is $\sum_kf'(k)x/f(k)\asymp x\log x$. The exponent $\frac1{4d-1}$ comes from balancing two terms. The first is the bound $x^{1+\eps}Z^{2-1/d}$ for the initial moduli; it arises from multiplying the full-variance bound \eqref{eq:full-variance} by the largest weight $f'(k)\asymp Z^{1-1/d}$. The second is the averaging error $x^2Z^{-1/(2d)}$ of \cref{prop:averaging} at $R=Z^{1/d}$. Equating $1+\theta(2-\frac1d)$ with $2-\frac\theta{2d}$ gives $\theta=\frac{2d}{4d-1}$. Improving either the treatment of small moduli or the correlation estimate would widen the range of \cref{cor:range}. Neither improvement is attempted here.

\chapter{Proof of the main theorem}\label{ch:assembly}

We now combine \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial,prop:corr,prop:averaging,prop:Df,prop:Theta} and \cref{lem:integral-identity}. Throughout, $d=\deg f$,
\[
a=4d-1,\qquad\theta=\frac{2d}a,\qquad\eta=\eta_d=\min\Bigl\{\frac15,\frac1a\Bigr\},
\]
and $\eps$ with $0<\eps<\eta/2$ is fixed. We put $\eps_1=\eps/2$ and apply \cref{prop:reduction,prop:initial} with $\eps_1$ in place of $\eps$. Constants written $C_f$ depend only on $f$, constants written $C_{f,\eps}$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and both may change from line to line. (Archived source: proposition P7.)

\section{The variance on an interval of moduli}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:interval}
Let $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$, $2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$ and $2\le R\le x$, and let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)$ be as in \cref{prop:averaging}. Then
\[
\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Correlations.} For $z<k\le y$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ integers $h$ with $1\le h\le x/f(k)$, and each $m=hf(k)$ is an integer in $[1,x]$. By \cref{prop:corr}, replacing $C_x(m)$ by $(x-m)\Sing(m)$ costs at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{4/5}$ for each pair $(h,k)$. After multiplying by $f'(k)$ and summing over $h$, the cost is at most $K_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}f'(k)/f(k)$, and by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:S-M}
|S_f(x;z,y)-M_f(x;z,y)|\le2UK_{\mathrm c}\,x^{9/5}\log(2x).
\end{equation}
\emph{Averaging.} \Cref{prop:averaging} applies under exactly the present hypotheses and gives
\[
|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2\mathcal A,\qquad|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_f\mathcal A,
\]
where we used $\widetilde R_f=R_f$ (\cref{prop:Df}(d)).

\emph{Combination.} By \cref{prop:reduction}, the factor $2$ in front of $S_f$ and the factor $x^2$ in front of $T_f$ give
\begin{multline*}
\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-\bigl[cx(Y-Z)+2I_f(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr]\Bigr|\\
\le C_{f,\eps}\bigl(x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}\bigr)+4UK_{\mathrm c}x^{9/5}\log(2x)+3C_fx^2\mathcal A.
\end{multline*}
\emph{Exact cancellation.} By \cref{lem:integral-identity}, $2I_f(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)$. By the definition \eqref{eq:ThetaF} of $F_f$, with $c=\zeta(2)^{-1}$, direct subtraction gives
\[
x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)=-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y),
\]
because $x^2\cdot c/(x/Y)=cxY$ and the $B_f$-terms cancel. Hence the bracket equals $x^2(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z))$.
\end{proof}

\section{Choice of the cutoffs and the error budget}\label{sec:budget}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main1}]
Take
\[
Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
\]
Both exponents lie in $(0,1)$. Choose $x_0=x_0(f)\ge2$ so that $Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}$ and $R\ge2$ for $x\ge x_0$; then also $Z\le x$ and $R\le x$. By \cref{lem:poly}(a) there is a unique real $z\ge1$ with $f(z)=Z$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exponents}
\begin{gathered}
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a},\qquad1+\theta\Bigl(2-\frac1d\Bigr)=\frac{8d-3}a=2-\frac1a,\\
\Bigl(2-\frac1a\Bigr)-\Bigl(\frac12+\frac{3d}a\Bigr)=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}

\emph{Case $Y\ge Z$.} Then $z\le y$, and $V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y)$. Hence
\[
|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|\le V_f(x,z)+x^2|F_f(x/Z)|+\Bigl|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\bigl(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\bigr)\Bigr|.
\]
We bound every term; the table summarises the result.
\begin{itemize}
\item By \cref{prop:initial} and \eqref{eq:exponents}, $V_f(x,z)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$.
\item By \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Z\ge1$, $x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$, by \eqref{eq:exponents}.
\item By \cref{lem:interval} the remaining difference is at most $C_{f,\eps}$ times $x^{3/2+\eps_1}+xY^{1-1/d}+x^{9/5}\log(2x)+x^2\mathcal A$, and by \eqref{eq:exponents} and $R\le x$, $x^2\mathcal A\le x^{2-1/a}\bigl((\log2x)^2+(\log2x)^3\bigr)$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
origin & bound & comparison with $x^{2-\eta+\eps}$\\
\midrule
diagonal and mixed terms (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $x^{3/2+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac15<\frac12$\\
endpoint of $\sum f'(k)$ (\cref{prop:reduction}) & $xY^{1-1/d}\le x^{2-1/d}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a\le\frac1d$\\
correlations (\cref{prop:corr}) & $x^{9/5}\log(2x)$ & $\eta\le\frac15$, $\log2x\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
averaging (\cref{prop:averaging}) & $x^{2-1/a}(\log2x)^3$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$, $(\log2x)^3\ll_\eps x^{\eps}$\\
initial moduli (\cref{prop:initial}) & $x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
lower boundary of the profile & $x^{1/2+3d/a}\le x^{2-1/a}$ & $\eta\le\frac1a$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The logarithmic bounds come from \cref{lem:sums}(d). Every row is at most $C_{f,\eps}x^{2-\eta+\eps}$ for $x\ge2$, which proves \eqref{eq:main1} when $Y\ge Z$.

\emph{Case $Y<Z$.} Apply \cref{prop:initial} with $y$ in place of $z$; this is allowed since $y\ge1$ and $f(y)=Y\le x$. Because $2-1/d>0$,
\[
0\le V_f(x,y)\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Y^{2-1/d}\le C_{f,\eps}x^{1+\eps_1}Z^{2-1/d}=C_{f,\eps}x^{2-1/a+\eps_1}.
\]
Also $x/Y\ge1$, so \eqref{eq:F-asym} and \eqref{eq:exponents} give $x^2|F_f(x/Y)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\le C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}\le C_fx^{2-1/a}$. The triangle inequality and $\eta\le1/a$ give \eqref{eq:main1} in this case too.

All constants and $x_0$ depend only on $f$ and $\eps$, and real values of $y$ and $z$ need no separate treatment: the sums split exactly as $k\le z$ and $z<k\le y$, and the endpoint effects are contained in \cref{prop:reduction}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:main2}]
For every $Y\le x$, \eqref{eq:F-asym} with $H=x/Y\ge1$, multiplied by $x^2$, gives
\[
\bigl|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\bigr|\le C_fx^2(x/Y)^{-13/8}=C_fx^{3/8}Y^{13/8},
\]
since $x^2(x/Y)^{-3/2}=x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$. Combine this with \eqref{eq:main1}. The formulas \eqref{eq:K-intro} and \eqref{eq:R-intro} and the positivity of $K_f$ are \cref{prop:Df}(d),(f).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The archived assembly notes that the hypothesis $\eps<\eta_d/2$ is not used: the argument works for every $\eps>0$. We keep the hypothesis as stated.
\end{remark}

\section{Proof of \cref{cor:range}}\label{sec:corollary}

Let $0<\delta<\eta/3$, apply \eqref{eq:main2} with $\eps=\delta$ (admissible because $\delta<\eta/2$), and divide by $K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}$, which is positive by \cref{prop:Df}(f). For $x^{1-2\eta/3+\delta}\le Y\le x^{1-\delta}$ the two relative errors are
\[
\frac{x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}=\Bigl(\frac Yx\Bigr)^{1/8}\le x^{-\delta/8},\qquad
\frac{x^{2-\eta+\delta}}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}}\le x^{3/2-\eta+\delta-\frac32(1-\frac{2\eta}3+\delta)}=x^{-\delta/2}\le x^{-\delta/8}.
\]
Hence $|V_f(x,y)/(K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2})-1|\le C(f,\delta)x^{-\delta/8}$ for $x\ge x_0(f,\delta)$. The range is nonempty because $\delta<\eta/3$. This deduction is carried out in both archived integration reports, one of them with $\eps=\delta/2$; it is not part of an approved proposition (see \texttt{changes.md}). \qed

\section{Where the exponents come from}

The cap $\eta_d\le\frac15$ comes from summing the uniform correlation error $x^{4/5}$ of \cref{prop:corr} over all pairs $(h,k)$; the weighted number of these pairs is $\sum_kf'(k)x/f(k)\asymp x\log x$. The exponent $\frac1{4d-1}$ comes from balancing two terms. The first is the bound $x^{1+\eps}Z^{2-1/d}$ for the initial moduli; it arises from multiplying the full-variance bound \eqref{eq:full-variance} by the largest weight $f'(k)\asymp Z^{1-1/d}$. The second is the averaging error $x^2Z^{-1/(2d)}$ of \cref{prop:averaging} at $R=Z^{1/d}$. Equating $1+\theta(2-\frac1d)$ with $2-\frac\theta{2d}$ gives $\theta=\frac{2d}{4d-1}$. Improving either the treatment of small moduli or the correlation estimate would widen the range of \cref{cor:range}. Neither improvement is attempted here.

1	\chapter{Numerical evidence}\label{ch:numerics}
2	
3	This chapter compares \cref{thm:main} with exact computations of $V_f(x,y)$. The computations come from the numerical snapshot accepted for the archived run (\texttt{source/numerics/snapshot}). Every number in the tables and figures below is recomputed by \texttt{reproduce.py} from that snapshot's own source code and from the formulas of \cref{ch:dirichlet,ch:mellin}; see the \texttt{README.md} accompanying this document. None of the numbers is part of the proof. The fits and their uncertainty envelopes are heuristic.
4	
5	\section{What is computed}
6	
7	The snapshot treats $f(t)=t^2+1$, $t^3+2$ and $2t+1$, which satisfy \eqref{eq:f-hyp}, for
8	\[
9	x\in\{2.5,5\}\cdot10^5\cup\{1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,256\}\cdot10^6
10	\]
11	and the target ratios $r\in\{0.01,0.02,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.4,0.7,1\}$; for each pair, $y$ is the largest integer with $f(y)\le rx$. At the two largest values of $x$ the extra ratio $r=0.005$ is also computed, as a diagnostic. The normalised value
12	\[
13	N_{\mathrm{data}}=\frac{V_f(x,y)}{x^{1/2}f(y)^{3/2}}
14	\]
15	is compared with the prediction
16	\[
17	N_{\mathrm{pred}}=F_f(H)H^{3/2}=\frac{x^2F_f(x/Y)}{x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}},\qquad H=\frac x{f(y)}.
18	\]
19	By \eqref{eq:F-asym}, $N_{\mathrm{pred}}\to K_f$ as $H\to\infty$.
20	
21	\paragraph{Algorithm of the snapshot.} The computation follows the expansion of \cref{ch:variance} exactly, with no approximation in the counts.
22	\begin{itemize}
23	\item The squarefree indicator up to $x$ is sieved, and all correlations $C_x(m)$, $0\le m\le x$, are obtained at once from one number-theoretic-transform autocorrelation modulo the prime $3221225473$. Every correlation is at most $x$, which is below the prime, so no information is lost. Then $\sum_lQ(x;q,l)^2=Q(x;1,1)+2\sum_{m\ge1}C_x(mq)$ by \cref{lem:pairs}.
24	\item With $g(q,l)=c\,h(q,l)$, where $h$ is the rational number given by \eqref{eq:density-closed}, the coefficients $B_q=\sum_lQ(x;q,l)h(q,l)$ and $D_q=\sum_lh(q,l)^2$ are computed as exact rationals. $B_q$ is computed from the counts $S_a=Q(x;a,0)$ exactly as in the proof of \cref{lem:mixed}. $D_q$ is computed from the local factors of \cref{prop:second-moment}(a): $p(p^2+p-1)/((p-1)(p+1)^2)$ for $p\parallel q$ and $p^2/(p^2-1)$ for $p^2\mid q$, divided by $q$.
25	\item The weighted sums are combined as $V=\sum_kf'(k)\bigl(\sum_lQ^2-2cxB_{f(k)}+c^2x^2D_{f(k)}\bigr)$ in 70-digit decimal arithmetic, with $c=6/\pi^2$ evaluated to 85 digits. The integer parts are exact; $V$ itself is irrational, so it is represented by a 70-digit approximation.
26	\end{itemize}
27	
28	\paragraph{Validation in the snapshot code.} The pipeline checks that the transform prime and its primitive root are valid. It checks the rational density formula against an independent enumeration of local residue conditions for all $1275$ pairs $(q,l)$ with $q\le50$, and against brute-force frequencies at $x=10^6$. It checks $\sum_lQ(x;q,l)=Q(x;1,1)$, and it compares, for every modulus at $x=257$, the exact $\sum_lQ^2$ and both rational coefficients with direct residue counts. For every production value of $x$ it also checks $C_x(0)$ and seven lags of the autocorrelation directly. All checks passed in the recomputation.
29	
30	\paragraph{Reproduction.} \texttt{reproduce.py} copies the snapshot's \texttt{compute.py} and \texttt{counts.cpp} unchanged, after checking their SHA-256 hashes against the acceptance record, compiles the C++ worker locally, and runs the snapshot pipeline on the full grid. In the run used to prepare this document, all $270$ recomputed rows agreed exactly with the archived results: the integer counts were identical, and so were the 70-digit values of $V$. This comparison is recorded in \texttt{reproduction.json}.
31	
32	\section{The constants}
33	
34	\Cref{tab:constants} lists $R_f$, $B_f$, $H_f(-\frac12)$ and $K_f$, computed from the Euler products of \cref{prop:Df} over the primes $p\le\Pmax$. The root counts $\rho(p)$ and $\rho(p^2)$ are computed by direct enumeration for small $p$ (for $\rho(p^2)$, $p\le300$; for $\rho(p)$, $p\le1000$). For larger $p$ they follow from the classical rules: for $t^2+1$, $\rho(p)=2$ if $p\equiv1\bmod4$ and $0$ otherwise; for $t^3+2$, $\rho(p)=1$ if $p\equiv2\bmod3$, and if $p\equiv1\bmod3$, $\rho(p)=3$ or $0$ according as $(-2)^{(p-1)/3}\equiv1\bmod p$ or not; for $2t+1$ and $t+1$, $\rho(p)=1$. For these $p$ the roots are simple, so $\rho(p^2)=\rho(p)$ by Hensel's lemma. The rules are checked against the direct counts wherever both are available.
35	
36	\begin{table}[ht]
37	\centering
38	\input{generated/tab_constants.tex}
39	\caption{Constants of \cref{thm:main}, Euler products over $p\le\Pmax$. The row $f(t)=t+1$ is the comparison of \cref{rem:vaughan}.}\label{tab:constants}
40	\end{table}
41	
42	\paragraph{Truncation.} $R_f$ and $B_f$ are computed from products and sums whose factors differ from $1$ by $O(p^{-3})$ or less, so their truncation errors are negligible at this precision. For $K_f$ the factor $M_p(-\frac12)$ differs from $1$ by about $(3+\rho(p))p^{-2}$. We therefore evaluate $\zeta(2)^{-3}\prod_pM_p(-\frac12)(1-p^{-2})^{-3}$, which is the same number. If $p\ge5$ and $\rho(p),\rho(p^2)\le3$, as is the case for $p>3$ for all four polynomials, then multiplying out the formula in \cref{prop:Df}(f) gives
43	\[
44	M_p(-\tfrac12)-1=-\frac{3+\rho(p)}{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p)}{p^{5/2}}+\frac{2+\rho(p)}{p^3}-\frac{\rho(p)+\rho(p^2)}{p^{7/2}}+\rho(p^2)\Bigl(\frac1{p^4}+\frac1{p^{9/2}}-\frac1{p^5}\Bigr),
45	\]
46	and hence $|M_p(-\frac12)-1|\le p^{-2}(6+3\cdot5^{-1/2}+1+6\cdot5^{-3/2}+0.2)\le10p^{-2}$. Since $(1-p^{-2})^{-3}\le1.131$ and $(1-p^{-2})^{-3}-1\le3.6p^{-2}$, it follows that $|M_p(-\frac12)(1-p^{-2})^{-3}-1|\le15p^{-2}$. By \cref{lem:products}(b) and \cref{lem:sums}(c), the omitted primes change $K_f$ by a relative amount of at most $e^{15/N}-1=\Ktrunc$ for $N=\Pmax$. This bound covers the truncation only; floating-point rounding is not certified by interval arithmetic. \Cref{tab:truncation} shows the values at three cutoffs. They are consistent with an actual truncation error far below this bound.
47

49	\centering
50	\input{generated/tab_truncation.tex}
51	\caption{$K_f$ with Euler products truncated at different prime cutoffs.}\label{tab:truncation}
52	\end{table}
53	
54	\paragraph{Vaughan's constant.} Evaluating \eqref{eq:c2} with the same cutoff gives $c_2\approx\cVaughan$, in agreement with $K_{t+1}=\KVau$, as \cref{rem:vaughan} predicts.
55	
56	\paragraph{Checks of \cref{prop:Df,prop:Theta}.} \texttt{reproduce.py} compares $\sum_{h\le2\cdot10^5}W_f(h)h^{-3}$ with $\zeta(3)P_f(3)$ and finds agreement to within the truncation error. \Cref{tab:theta} shows the normalised remainder $(\Theta_f(H)-R_fH^2\log H-B_fH^2-cH)/H^{1/2}$, which by \eqref{eq:Theta} equals $-K_f+O(H^{-1/8})$. It visibly approaches $-K_f$.

59	\centering
60	\input{generated/tab_theta.tex}
61	\caption{$(\Theta_f(H)-R_fH^2\log H-B_fH^2-cH)/H^{1/2}$ compared with $-K_f$.}\label{tab:theta}
62	\end{table}

64	\section{The data against the profile}
65	
66	\Cref{tab:profile} compares the data at the largest $x=\xmaxdata$ with the profile, and \cref{fig:profile} plots both together with the limit $K_f$. \Cref{fig:deviation} shows how the relative deviation evolves with $x$; the full data are in \cref{app:tables}.
67	
68	\begin{table}[ht]
69	\centering
70	\small
71	\input{generated/tab_profile.tex}
72	\caption{Normalised variance at $x=\xmaxdata$ against the predicted profile $N_{\mathrm{pred}}=F_f(H)H^{3/2}$, $H=x/f(y)$; $r$ is the target ratio.}\label{tab:profile}
73	\end{table}

75	\begin{figure}[ht]
76	\centering
77	\input{generated/fig_profile.tex}
78	\caption{Predicted profile $F_f(1/r)\,r^{-3/2}$ (solid), data at $x=\xmaxdata$ (circles) and the constant $K_f$ (dashed), against $r=f(y)/x$ on a logarithmic axis.}\label{fig:profile}
79	\end{figure}

81	\begin{figure}[ht]
82	\centering
83	\input{generated/fig_deviation.tex}
84	\caption{Relative deviation $100(N_{\mathrm{data}}/N_{\mathrm{pred}}-1)$ against $x$, one line per target ratio $r$.}\label{fig:deviation}
85	\end{figure}
86	
87	The observations are as follows.
88	\begin{itemize}
89	\item For $f(t)=2t+1$, where $y$ is large ($y$ between $\YminLin$ and $\YmaxLin$ at the largest $x$), data and profile agree to within $\DevmaxLin\%$.
90	\item For $f(t)=t^2+1$ ($y$ between $\YminTwo$ and $\YmaxTwo$), the deviation lies between $\DevminTwo\%$ and $\DevmaxTwo\%$. At every ratio it has decreased by more than an order of magnitude from the smallest to the largest $x$.
91	\item For $f(t)=t^3+2$, $y$ is only $\YminThree$--$\YmaxThree$, and the deviation ranges from $\DevminThree\%$ to $\DevmaxThree\%$, the largest value occurring at the diagnostic ratio $0.005$. It has decreased substantially over the range of $x$, from more than $10\%$ at the smallest $x$ for small ratios. Between the two largest $x$ it decreased at eight of the nine ratios. This behaviour is compatible with large lower-order terms from the sampling of $k$, which the proof controls only through the $Z^{-1/d}$ terms of \cref{prop:averaging}. That explanation is plausible but has not been proved.

93	The theorem's error bound is far from small in this range. Relative to the main term it is about $x^{-\eta_d}r^{-3/2}$, and at $x=2.56\cdot10^8$ already $x^{-1/11}\approx0.17$ for $d=3$ and $x^{-1/7}\approx0.06$ for $d=2$. The data are therefore consistent with the theorem, and they agree with the predicted profile far better than the proved error term requires. However, they cannot test the error exponent.

95	\section{Extrapolation to small ratios}
96	
97	The snapshot also estimates the small-ratio constant empirically. Among the eight target ratios it selects the smallest one, $0.01$ for all three polynomials, such that all rows at this or a larger ratio changed by less than $1\%$ between the two largest $x$. It then fits $N(r)=C+a\sqrt r+br$ by unweighted least squares to the largest-$x$ rows with $r\ge0.01$, using the actual ratios. The reported uncertainty is the maximum of twice the formal standard error and of the shifts under several variations: of the cutoff, of $x$, of the model, and of the fitted ratio window. It is a heuristic sensitivity envelope, not a confidence interval.

100	\centering
101	\input{generated/tab_extrapolation.tex}
102	\caption{The snapshot's extrapolation $C_{\mathrm{fit}}$ with its heuristic envelope, the same fit applied to the exact profile $N_{\mathrm{pred}}$ at the same ratios, and the constant $K_f$.}\label{tab:extrapolation}
103	\end{table}

More informative is the third column. Applying the same fit to the \emph{exact} predicted profile at the same ratios reproduces the data intercepts closely ($\CpredTwo$, $\CpredThree$, $\CpredLin$ against $\CfitTwo$, $\CfitThree$, $\CfitLin$). The gap between $C_{\mathrm{fit}}$ and $K_f$ is therefore a bias of the three-parameter model, not a discrepancy between data and theory. By \eqref{eq:F-asym} the profile approaches $K_f$ with a relative correction of order $r^{1/8}$, which a model in $\sqrt r$ and $r$ fitted on $r\ge0.01$ cannot capture. \Cref{fig:profile} shows how slowly the profile flattens.

At fixed ratio, $V_f\approx x^2F_f(1/r)$, so the slope in $x$ is $2$, and the fits find $\alpha+\beta\approx2$. Over the finite ratio range, however, the profile is not a pure power of $r$, so the fixed-$x$ exponent $\beta$ and the joint exponents do not recover $\frac32$ and $\frac12$.

113	\end{table}

115	\section{Limitations}
116	
117	The numerical evidence concerns three polynomials and $x\le2.56\cdot10^8$. In the cubic case, $y$ is small and the agreement is only at the per-cent level. All uncertainties attached to fits are heuristic. The snapshot's validation tests the implementation on small cases and spot checks, not every production count. In the recomputation, every archived row was reproduced exactly; this confirms reproducibility, not the correctness of the shared code. The constants are computed in double precision from truncated Euler products, with a rigorous bound for the truncation of $K_f$ but without certified rounding.

# Changes and source map

Archive: `source/` (run `zt-thesis-plan`, plan `thesis@gpt-6.1-sol`, archive
commit `867fc9baf25edf4995748d91dd950e98cfd9debf`). Every proposition P1–P7 is
archived as `source/props/Pn/statement.md` and `source/props/Pn/proof.md`, with
two reviews: `review-v1-0.json` by `claude-opus-5-5` and `review-v1-1.json` by
`codex:gpt-6.1-sol`. All fourteen reviews give the verdict **pass**. Their
severities are "none", except "cosmetic" for the Opus reviews of P2, P5 and P7.
The integration reports are `source/report/assembly-claude-opus-5-5.md`,
`assembly-codex-gpt-6.1-sol.md`, `integration*.json`; both conclude that the
propositions compose with no loss.

No mathematical correction was made, and no gap was found. No `brief.md`,
`feedback/` or `build-feedback.txt` was supplied, and the intervention record
(`source/interventions.md`) authorises no change to the mathematics.

## 1. Map of results

Numbers refer to the compiled `main.pdf`. "Pn (k)" means equation (k) of the archived proof of Pn.

| Manuscript | Archived source | Reviews |
|---|---|---|
| Theorem 1.1 (main theorem), (1.8)–(1.11) | P7 statement; plan main theorem (`source/plan.md`); constants from P5 statement, (29), (34) | P7 v1-0, v1-1; P5 v1-0, v1-1 |
| Corollary 1.2 | plan main theorem ("In particular…"); derived in both integration reports (Opus with ε=δ, Sol with ε=δ/2); **not** an approved proposition | — (integration reports) |
| Remark 1.3 (two regimes) | integration report (Sol), last paragraph of numerics section; plan "Numerics check" | — |
| Remark 1.4 (K_{t+1}=c_2) | **added in write-up** (see §5) | — |
| Remark 1.5 (limitations), §9.4 | integration reports, "loss_vs_plan"; plan risks of P3, P7 | — |
| §1.5 strategy | plan summary and statements P1–P7 | — |
| Lemma 2.1 (elementary sums) | P1 (19), (21); P2 (17) and the bound for log(2x); P3 (3), (15)–(16); P4 (34); P5 (2) | P1–P5 reviews |
| Lemma 2.2 (divisor bound) | P2 (5); P3 (2) (special case η=1/10) | P2, P3 |
| Lemma 2.3 (infinite products) | P5 (3) and the positivity argument after (27); P1 convergence of ∏(1−2/p²) after (28); the Cauchy argument comes from the cosmetic remark of P5 review v1-0 | P5 v1-0 (cosmetic) |

| Chapter 10 | numerical snapshot `source/numerics/snapshot/` (README, report, compute.py, counts.cpp); plan "Numerics check"; integration reports' numerics sections | — |
| Appendix A | snapshot `results.json` (recomputed) | — |
| Appendix B | `provenance.json`, `source/interventions.md`, `source/numerics/accepted.json` | — |

## 2. Notation changes

- Polynomial growth constants: P2's `A, B`, P4's `a, B` and P7's `b_f, B_f^*` became κ₁, κ₂ (Lemma 2.6). This avoids a clash with the constant B_f. U = κ₂/κ₁ and V = U+U² come from P4 (3).
- P2's mixed term `M(x;q)` → Δ(x;q). P2's `N_a(x), D_a` → Q(x;a,0), g(a,0).
- P4's tail and moment `T_R, M_R` → 𝒯(R), 𝒩(R). P4's `D = U+V` → D_w. P4's `K, K_2` → K₂, K₃. P4's `S_1, S_2, I_2` → T_f, M_f, I_f, which are also P7's `M, I`. P4's `H = ⌊x/Z⌋` → H₀.
- P4's coefficient `R_f = Σ λ(r)ρ(r)/r` is written R̃_f in Chapter 6 until Proposition 7.2(d) identifies it with the residue R_f. The archive uses one symbol, and P5 proves the equality.
- P3: divisor variables `d, e` → e₁, e₂ (d is the degree); `A(m), A_H(m)` → 𝒜(m), 𝒜_H(m); constant `67+2D` → K_c = 67+2D_{1/10}.
- P5: the local coefficients α_p, β_p, δ_p of P5 (4) are used throughout. The local factor of P_f is L_p(s) and that of H_f is M_p(s) (P5 notation). P6's local factor of H_f, written `L_p` there, is M_p here. The archived a_p, b_p, c_p and B_p(s) are recorded in §7.2 of the manuscript.
- P6: the constant of MV Cor. 10.5, called `Q` there, → c_MV.
- P7: δ = ε/2 → ε₁ (δ is reserved for Corollary 1.2).
- P1: the auxiliary `L(r) = φ(r)G(r)²` is not used. The text works with λ/c² directly, as P4 does.
- W_f(h) is displayed in the introduction by its three local cases (1.5). These cases are those of P5 after (5). K_f is displayed in the expanded form (1.10), which is algebraically identical to P5 (29): (1−2/p²)[a_p+(b_p−a_p)√p+(c_p−b_p)p] = α_p+β_p√p+δ_p p, and the expansion was checked with sympy.

## 3. Merged arguments

- **Counting squarefree numbers in a class**: P2 (6) is P1 (5) with l = 0, because N_a(x) = Q(x;a,0) and D_a = g(a,0). Both now cite Proposition 3.1.
- **Polynomial bounds**: P2 §1, P4 (1)–(5) and P7 (1)–(2) are merged into Lemma 2.6. P2's bound Σ f'(k)/f(k) ≤ (3D_ηB/A)L log(2x) is replaced by P4's 2U log(2x) (Lemma 2.6(c)). This changes only the constant in Proposition 4.3.
- **Divisor bound**: P2 (5) and P3 (2) are merged into Lemma 2.2.
- **Ramanujan sums**: P1 (24)–(25) and P4 (12)–(15) are merged into Lemma 2.5. Multiplicativity is proved via (a) as a Dirichlet convolution (the P4 route), which replaces P1's CRT sketch (P1 review v1-0, cosmetic).
- **Zeta formula**: P5 (22) and P6 (3) are the same identity and are merged into (7.1).
- **Infinite products and Euler products**: the convergence arguments repeated in P1, P3, P4 and P5 are merged into Lemmas 2.3 and 2.4.
- **Root-count bounds**: P5 (1) and P6 (6) are merged into Lemma 2.7.

## 4. Editorial completions and choices (no change to statements)

1. Lemma 2.3(a): the convergence of the partial products is proved by a Cauchy argument. P5 only bounded the tails; P5 review v1-0 flagged this as cosmetic and trivially fillable.
2. Propositions 3.2(b), 3.3 and Lemma 6.2: the text states explicitly that λ, γ², λβ are c² times multiplicative functions (λ(1) = c²) before taking Euler products. The archive's "absolutely convergent multiplicative series" is the same argument.
3. Lemma 6.3: the bound |w(y)| ≤ U/y ≤ U/z is made explicit (P4 review v1-0, cosmetic).
4. Proposition 5.1: the unused remark about √x terms is dropped (P3 review v1-0, cosmetic). The proposition is stated in P3's stronger proved form (absolute constant, x^{4/5}). The archived contract form C(ε)x^{4/5+ε} is recorded as a consequence. The circle-method cutoff mentioned in the P3 contract is "permitted" and is not used by the proof; the text says so.
5. P3 lists P1 as a dependency, but the proof does not use it (assembly report Opus, cosmetic). The manuscript notes only that P3 is self-contained.
6. Lemma 9.1 uses P3's proved bound x^{4/5} (no ε) and obtains x^{9/5} log(2x) in place of P7's x^{9/5+δ} log(2x). The final error terms are unchanged.
7. Proposition 6.4 keeps the archived error 𝒜 with (log 2R)² factors, although Proposition 3.2(d) (P1) proves the bounds for 𝒯, 𝒩 without logarithms, as P1's proof notes.
8. Proposition 7.2(b): for fixed σ the bound is exp(E_H(σ)) with E_H(σ) = Σ_p sup|M_p−1|. This is P5 (12)–(13) without the explicit term list. In (b) the bound |α_p − 1| ≤ 2p^{-2} is used, which follows from (7.4); P5 used 2p^{-2}+C₀p^{-3}.
9. Lemma 8.3 (uniform bound for H_f on −5/8 ≤ Re s ≤ 2): this is the argument of P6 (6)–(9), written with α_p, β_p, δ_p. The term-by-term bookkeeping gives |M_p − 1| ≤ (4+4d)p^{-3/2} and M_H = e^{8(1+d)}∏_{p∈𝓑}(1+p^{-3/4})(1+p^{5/8}+p^{5/4}), in place of P6's (6+17d)p^{-3/2} and its U_p. Each inequality was re-verified; the structure and conclusion are those of P6.
10. Chapter 8: the holomorphy of ζ in the strip is taken from Lemma 7.1(b) (P5's continuation) instead of being deduced from MV Cor. 10.4 as in P6 §1. Cor. 10.5 is still quoted, and Cor. 10.4 is mentioned as its origin. The introduction says that two results are quoted (BGPVW Lemma 2.2, MV Cor. 10.5).
11. Lemma 8.4: the bound on the horizontal segments is stated as O_v(T^{-3}). P6 review v1-0 noted, as cosmetic, that the bound for |v^z| was not written out.
12. Chapter 9 keeps the hypothesis 0<ε<η_d/2 of the statement and adds a remark that the argument does not use it (P7 review v1-0, cosmetic).
13. Prose: background (Chapter 1) on Vaughan's theorem (k=2 case of Vaughan 2005, (1.13)–(1.15)), on Brüdern–Wooley and on the Goldston–Vaughan method is taken from the introductions of the supplied papers. Mirsky (1949) is cited from the bibliography candidate list as background for correlations of squarefree numbers; its content was not checked.

## 5. Material added while preparing the write-up

- **Remark 1.4 (consistency with Vaughan's constant).** For ρ ≡ 1 (f(t)=t+1) each local factor of (1.10) equals (1−p^{-2})² times the local factor of Vaughan's C₁ (Vaughan 2005, (1.15), k=2). This was verified symbolically with sympy, treating √p as a variable. Hence K_{t+1} = c₂. The numerical values are computed by `reproduce.py` (Table 10.1, `reproduction.json` → `vaughan_c2`). The remark is only a consistency check, not part of the proof.

The bound |M_p(−½) − 1| ≤ 10p^{-2} (p ≥ 5, ρ ≤ 3) uses the explicit expansion displayed in §10.2, which was checked with sympy. The resulting relative bound is e^{15/N} − 1. The Opus integration report used a similar bound (15/p², for the unnormalised factors).
- **Numerical checks in Chapter 10**: D_f(3) vs ζ(3)P_f(3); the normalised remainder of Θ_f (Table 10.3); the comparison of data with the profile x²F_f(x/Y) (Table 10.4, Figures 10.1–10.2); and the snapshot extrapolation applied to the exact profile (Table 10.5). The last two analyses appear in the Opus integration report, where they were done with scripts that are not archived. They were re-implemented in `reproduce.py`, and all values in the manuscript come from that script. The reproduced values agree with those quoted in the integration report (for example, the fitted profile intercepts 0.134364, 0.135793, 0.141685 and the deviation ranges at x = 2.56·10^8).
- **Reproduction of the snapshot**: `reproduce.py` reruns the archived snapshot code. In the run used for this document, all 270 rows (3 polynomials × 90 rows, including the diagnostic ratio) agreed exactly with the archived `results.json`.

## 6. Items checked and left unchanged

- The quotations of BGPVW Lemma 2.2, (2.6), (2.7) (P2) and of MV Corollaries 10.4–10.5 (P6) were compared with the supplied PDFs and match.
- Every proof was re-read step by step while writing. The writer found no gap, sign error, range error or missing uniformity, so no `SOURCE_GAP.md` was written.

\chapter{Provenance of this document}\label{app:provenance}

\paragraph{Source.} This document presents the proof recorded in an archived run of the project repository
\begin{center}\url{https://gitlab.com/mshepherd/squarefree-numbers}.\end{center}
The run is labelled \texttt{zt-thesis-plan}, and the archive commit is
\begin{center}\texttt{867fc9baf25edf4995748d91dd950e98cfd9debf}\end{center}
(the harness commit is the same). The run followed the plan \texttt{thesis@gpt-6.1-sol}. Of the competing plans, this one was selected by Markus Schepke, the project owner. It decomposes the problem into seven propositions P1--P7, which correspond to \cref{ch:densities,ch:variance,ch:correlations,ch:averaging,ch:dirichlet,ch:mellin,ch:assembly}. For this run the problem statement was accompanied by a short hint, written by the run operator with the project owner's authorisation, that pointed towards Vaughan's paper \cite{vaughan2005} and the work of Brüdern and Wooley \cite{bruedernwooley2011} without describing a method. The numerical snapshot was reused, with the owner's authorisation, from the numerics stage of an earlier run of the same problem. Its acceptance record describes it as ``operator selected; not a proof of numerical correctness''.

\paragraph{Status of the evidence.} Each of P1--P7 was approved in its first version by two independent model referees, one from each model family; their reports are archived next to the proofs. Both integration reports concluded that the propositions compose to the main theorem without loss. This agreement between models is evidence, not certification. While preparing this document, every argument was rechecked step by step, and no mathematical gap was found. The changes made are editorial: notation, merging of repeated arguments into shared lemmas, a few explicit intermediate steps, and the fuller statement of some constants. \Cref{rem:vaughan}, the truncation bound and the consistency checks in \cref{ch:numerics}, and the corresponding parts of \texttt{reproduce.py} were added while preparing this document.
